Stores the count in $0C6F, places the enemies ($14FB), then sets two colours of the play palette by the count, entry (count - 1) AND 7: $86A0 (colour 3) from $14D4 and $869F (colour 2) from $14F3. The BBC wrote BBC colour numbers into its own palette table; the C64 tables hold C64 colour codes and its palette is at $869D. Called from the preview ($8858) and the next-landscape routine ($1A9D).

Makes the player's robot and puts it on the landscape. Takes a new object number for a robot ($211D, A = 0) into $0B and sets the starting energy $0C0A to 10. On landscape 0000 ($0C52 = 0) it stands the robot on tile x 8, z 17 ($1F16) and jumps to the tree placement at $147D; otherwise it has $1238 put it on a random flat, empty tile lower than min(6, $0C06), the lowest enemy's height ($1238 raises its limit after every 255 failed tries), repeating until that succeeds, and falls into $147D. Called from the preview ($886C) and from $1AA0. The BBC routine.

Adds the trees. Limit $75 = 48 - 3 x the enemy count ($0C6F); count = 10 + a seed number 0-22 ($3451), no more than the limit, kept in $1E. Each tree takes a new object number ($211D, A = 2) and goes on a random flat, empty tile lower than the lowest enemy's height $0C06 ($1238); the first failure ends the loop. Falls through into make_secret_code ($14AA). The BBC routine.

Runs the landscape's seed sequence on to its secret code and checks the code typed in. X counts 170 down to 128 (from 165 when $0C71 bit 7 is set, as after a won landscape: the display code at $33C4-$33D5 then makes the last four numbers itself). Each step takes the next seed number as BCD ($339A), compares it with the byte at $0C6F+X (for X = 132-129 the four typed pairs at $0CF3-$0CF0), rotates the match into $0C65, and stores the difference plus the byte at $0100 ($7F, the flags of object 0, the Sentinel on its tower) at $3F00+Y, Y starting from the landscape's offset $0C55 and wrapping within page $3F. On the C64 page $3F is the run-once start-up code at $3F00-$3FB3, so playing a landscape overwrites 43 of its bytes; on the BBC the page was a screen buffer. During play $254F-$2570 reads five of them back: the four for the typed pairs must be $7F, the one before them must not. Then ASL $0C71: bit 7 was set - return ($14D3); clear - on to $14DC.

Colour 3 of the play palette for enemy counts 1-8, as C64 colour codes: 5 green, 2 red, 7 yellow, 3 cyan, 2 red, 3 cyan, 2 red, 7 yellow (read at $1443, stored in $86A0). The BBC table gave the same colours as BBC colour numbers (2, 1, 3, 6, 1, 6, 1, 3).

End of the secret-code check, when the landscape is about to be played. Unless bits 1-4 of $0C65 are all set (all four typed pairs matched) it returns through $14D3, and the preview goes on to the wrong-code screen ($886F, $1074). On a match it drops its own return address and returns instead into the game start at $356D, through an address computed from $0100: high = $0100 + $B6, low = high + $37, which is $356C only when $0100 holds $7F. The BBC's second constant was $6E, for its game start at $35A4.

Colour 2 of the play palette for enemy counts 1-8, as C64 colour codes: 1 white, 7 yellow, 3 cyan, 2 red, 1 white, 7 yellow, 3 cyan, 2 red (read at $1449, stored in $869F). The BBC's numbers for the same colours were 7, 3, 6, 1, 7, 3, 6, 1.

Stands the Sentinel and sentries on the highest ground. $15CC first finds each 4x4 block's highest flat tile (height $AE10+b, tile $AE60+b / $AEA0+b) and the landscape's highest in $06. For each enemy n (count in $0C6F): type $0A40+n = 1 (sentry); lists the blocks at height $06 ($159D), lowering $06 a level ($10) while there are none; picks one of them with a seed number ($31CA) masked by $27 and less than the list length; zeroes that block's height and its eight neighbours' ($AE07-$AE19 + block) so no enemy lands next to another; uses the block's highest tile as (x, z). Enemy 0 is the Sentinel: tile noted in $0C19/$0C1A, type 5, and first a tower (type 6, facing 0) placed under it. Each enemy is placed ($1F16), its meanie records cleared ($1973), its tactics timer $0C30+n set to (seed / 2) AND 63 OR 5 and its turn step $9D37+n to +20 or -20 by the seed's bit 0. Ends with $0C06 = the last enemy's height (high nibble of $06). If $06 reaches 0 before every enemy has a block, $1515 sets the count $0C6F to the $FF that $159D leaves in X, not to the number placed. The BBC routine, tables moved +$5300.

Lists the 4x4 blocks whose highest flat tile ($AE10+b) equals the height in $06 (tile-byte form, height in the high nibble): block numbers to $AD40 onward, the count to $74, and to $27 the mask from $15C4 that just covers the count's highest set bit. Returns C clear when there is at least one, C set when there is none. X is $FF on return either way. The BBC routine, tables moved +$5300.

$FF $7F $3F $1F $0F $07 $03 $01: entry n has n leading zero bits. Indexed by the number of leading zeros of a count, it gives the smallest all-ones mask covering the count (read at $15BB for the block list and at $86B6 outside this range).

Splits the landscape into an 8 x 8 grid of 4x4-tile blocks (the last row and column one tile short, the landscape being 31 tiles across) and for block b = 0-63 records the height of its highest flat tile (shape 0) in $AE10+b and that tile's x and z in $AE60+b and $AEA0+b; a block without a flat tile keeps height 0. The highest of all ends up in $06. C64 difference: the tile routine $2BA8 only points $5E/$5F and Y at the tile byte, so this routine loads it itself (LDA ($5E),Y at $1601); the BBC's tile routine returned it in A.

Scanner refresh, run by the raster interrupt at most once a frame ($9666, together with the timer gate), or after each scroll step during a pan ($3687). While $0C04 is non-zero (an enemy is draining the player, set by check_player_drain) it redraws the scanner in that state; otherwise it redraws it in state 0 once, when the last state drawn ($0C09) was not 0. The BBC routine.

C64 rewrite of the scanner drawing. A = state: 0 off, 4 static (an enemy is draining the player), 8 solid (pause, from $34C8; $34D7 clears it). Stores it in $0C09 and $16A0, switches sprites 1-3 on for a non-zero state and off for 0 (bits 1-3 of $D015), then fills four rows of eight byte-columns of their sprite data: counter $169F runs 8 down to 1, column address $7000 + the byte at $16AC+counter ($7040-$7042 sprite 1, $7080-$7082 sprite 2, $70C0-$70C1 sprite 3, left to right), rows at +9, +6, +3, +0, each byte taken from $16A1 + state + two noise bits. The noise comes from page 2, 256 seed-generator numbers stored at start-up ($3FA0-$3FAF), read backwards through the operand at $1671. After the left four columns, if $0C4F is $40 (the enemy sees the player but not the player's tile) the rest is drawn in state 0: the half-full scanner. The BBC drew the same pattern into its bitmap, with fresh random numbers, at an address worked out from $0CC2.

Self-modified operand: the low byte of LDA $0200 at $1670, decremented at $166D before every read, so the scanner's noise walks down page 2 one byte per row, 32 bytes per redraw, wrapping within the page (0 in both snapshots). The code after it finishes draw_scanner's loop: two more DEYs make the row step 3, $1683 counts the columns, and $168F-$169B switches the right half to state 0 when $0C4F is $40.

Unused on the C64: no traced instruction reads or writes it, directly or through an index. It sits where the BBC kept the scanner's random number, which the C64 no longer needs because its noise comes from page 2.

draw_scanner's column counter, 8 down to 1 ($165C-$1688); just before the loop it briefly holds the sprite-enable bits ($0E or 0) that are merged into $D015 ($164C-$1657). C64 use of the BBC's block counter byte. 0 in both snapshots.

The state draw_scanner is filling with, 0, 4 or 8 (from A at $1642), ORed with two noise bits to index $16A1; set to 0 at $1698 for the right half when the player's tile is hidden from the enemy. 0 in both snapshots.

Sprite data bytes for the scanner, four per state, chosen by state + two noise bits: state 0 $55 $55 $55 $55 (every pixel pair %01), state 4 $B5 $75 $5B $57 (%01 with a few %10 and %11 pairs: the static), state 8 $FF $FF $FF $FF (every pair %11). C64 values for multicolour sprites; the BBC's twelve bytes were pixel bytes for its own screen.

Index base for the scanner's column addresses: draw_scanner reads $16AC + counter for counter 8 down to 1, so the table proper is $16AD-$16B4 = $C1 $C0 $82 $81 $80 $42 $41 $40, low bytes of $70xx in sprite data (sprite 1 at $7040, sprite 2 at $7080, sprite 3 at $70C0; counter 8 is the leftmost column). The byte at $16AC itself is the last state-8 fill byte. C64 addition.

One enemy's turn in the gameplay loop (called from $129F). Saves the stack pointer in $0C0D so that any routine below can abandon the turn ($1AF9). For the enemy numbered in $90 (0-7): the Sentinel (type 5) or a sentry (type 1) has its type put in $0C1C (the object the game-over screen shows, read at $87DA) and, if its object still exists, gets its tactics ($16E6); if its object slot is empty (absorbed, or never made on this landscape) it releases one unit of stored energy as a tree ($1A5D) and draws the tree ($1876). Other slots just end the turn ($16D6). The C64 keeps the enemy number in zero page $90 because $00 and $01 are the 6510's processor port; the BBC kept it in $00.

Ends an enemy's turn: takes one number from the seed generator ($31CA) to stir it, steps the enemy number in $90 down (7 after 0) and makes the player ($0B) the viewing object ($6E) again. Every exit of the tactics code comes here, including the abandon path at $1AF9.

What the Sentinel or a sentry (X = enemy 0-7) does on its turn. Acts only when its tactics timer $0C30+X has run down to 1; re-arms it to 4 and sets the view arc $0C68 to 20 yaw units (one screen width). Then, in order: a meanie it has made is handled first ($16FF); energy it holds is put back as a tree ($1773); it looks for a robot to drain ($1795) or else a tree or boulder ($17E0); failing all, it turns ($17F9). A target found goes to $1825 (drain timer, draining, meanie making) and every change is redrawn at $1876/$187B. The tactics timer values it sets: 4 by default, 10 after a meanie turns, 30 after a drain, 50 after making a meanie. The BBC routine except for $90/$91 in place of the BBC's $00/$01 and the two turning sounds ($1750, $181D), which the C64 plays by number alone where the BBC also passed two pitches in X and Y.

enemy_tactics, meanie part (A = the meanie's object, now the viewer in $6E). If its target robot ($0CA8+X) no longer exists, stops the enemy's drain timer and turns the meanie back into a tree ($1758). Otherwise it looks at the robot ($1887): outside its 20-unit arc it turns 8 units towards it ($0C0E = +8 or -8, $1728; sound 1 through $3470; tactics timer 10); inside, if the robot is the player's and the robot or its tile is visible ($14 non-zero) it forces a hyperspace ($2156) and puts 4, meanie, in $0C1C; if not the player's it becomes a tree again with the drain timer stopped, and if not visible, a tree again ($175D: type 2, $0CA0+X = $80).

enemy_tactics with no meanie: the enemy becomes the viewer ($6E) and releases one unit of any energy it holds as a tree ($1A5D); if that worked the turn ends by drawing the tree ($1876). Otherwise, when $0CB8+X bit 7 asks for it, it searches straight away for a tree or boulder to drain ($1AB0): found, it resets its meanie search start ($0C80+X = 64) and drains it ($17EA); not found, it clears that bit and goes on to $1795.

enemy_tactics, robot search. With its drain timer ($0C20+X) running it first re-checks its present target ($0CA8+X) and keeps it ($1825) if the target is still visible; otherwise stops the timer. Then it looks at all 64 objects as robots ($1887 with A = 0), from 63 down: the first robot whose tile it can see, with no tree in the way ($0C76 bit 6 clear), becomes the target ($1825); a player's robot seen without its tile is remembered in $0F. If only that was found, and the player is not the target it last failed to make a meanie for ($0C90+X), it clears its meanie records ($1973) and takes the player as target with visibility $40. Otherwise ($17E0) it stops the drain timer and looks for a tree or boulder to drain ($1AB0); if there is one it drains it ($1A08, tactics timer 30); if not, it may turn ($17F9).

enemy_tactics, turning: once the turn timer $0C28+X has run down to 1 (otherwise the turn ends, $1802), and if the change may be drawn now ($1AF4), adds the enemy's step $9D37+X (+20 or -20 units of a 256-unit circle) to its yaw $09C0+X, sets the turn timer to 200, clears its meanie records ($1973), plays sound 0 ($3470; the BBC also passed pitches 7 and 120 in X and Y) and redraws it at once ($187B).

enemy_tactics with a target in Y: records it in $0CA8+X and its visibility ($14) in $0CB0+X. A stopped drain timer ($0C20+X = 0) is started at 120 and the turn ends; a timer still above 1 ends the turn. At 1: if the target's tile is visible ($14 bit 7) the enemy drains it ($1A08), sets its tactics timer to 30 and redraws the object unless it was the player; if only the robot is visible it goes on to make a meanie ($1852).

enemy_tactics, meanie making: $1986 looks for a tree near the target. Success: tactics timer 50 and the new meanie ($0CA0+Y) drawn dithered ($1876). Failure: if the enemy has failed fewer than two times ($0C98+Y), $0CB8+Y bit 7 is set so its next turn looks for a tree or boulder to drain; otherwise its drain timer is stopped.

Shared exit of the tactics code: $1876 first sets $0C6D to $40 (the BBC's flag for a dithered redraw); $187B, used after turns, does not. Both make object X the current object ($91; the BBC used $01), the player the viewer, redraw it ($1F9F) and end the turn ($16D6).

Can the viewing object ($6E, an enemy or a meanie) see object Y, which must be of type A? Returns $14 with bit 7 set if it can see the object's tile and, for a robot, bit 6 if it can see the robot itself; $0C76 gets the corresponding tree-in-the-way bits. C is set only when the object is outside the viewer's arc ($0C68). X and Y are kept (X in $191E; Y also left in $0C58). Clears $14, gives up (C clear) if object Y is unused or of another type, gets the angles to it ($8401), then passes through an anti-cracker step ($18A2) into the arc and gaze checks ($18B8). The BBC routine with its callees moved.

Anti-cracker step run on every sight check: $0C75 = the byte at $0F3D + 7 if its low digit is 9, else + 1, so $0C75 always ends up the larger. $0F3D is the operand of LDA #$00 at $0F3C, written by $2C5F; the check at $322F (X = 7 from $322D) calls $31A2 when $0C75 is below it. Same as the BBC.

Second half of check_enemy_sight. Leaves with C set when the object's yaw from the viewer ($0C57) is outside the arc: $0C57 - 10 + $0C68/2 must be below $0C68 (20 for enemies and meanies, 40 in the meanie-tree search). Otherwise copies the ground-plane angle $8A/$8B to the gaze yaw $3D/$3E and makes one trace, or two for a robot ($4C = 0; counter $1E): first at the robot itself with $0C6E bit 7 set, then at its tile, 224/256 of a tile lower. Each trace gets the pitch from the height difference ($933D), builds the gaze vector ($1C54), follows it ($1CDD) and rotates the results into $14 (target seen, from $0C56) and $0C76 (tree seen, from $0CDD). Ends with C clear.
Where check_enemy_sight keeps X from entry ($1889) to exit ($1917), so X comes back unchanged.

Is an enemy draining the player? Looks at objects 0-7 for a Sentinel or sentry (types 5 and 1) whose target ($0CA8+n) is the player's robot ($0B) and whose drain timer ($0C20+n) is running. Found: $0C04 = 4 (the scanner fills with static) and $0C4F = that enemy's view of the player ($0CB0+n: $80 tile visible, $40 robot only); one that sees the tile ends the search, one that sees only the robot lets it go on. None: both 0. Then puts 4 or 0 in the sound selector $0C73, and if that changed and the old value was not 3, silences SID voice 2 (OSBYTE $15 with X = 1 through $3527). Called from the gameplay loop ($12BB). C64 changes: the old selector is kept in $1972 and reloaded (the BBC kept it in A), the flags are saved around the store with PHP/PLP (not needed: STY leaves them alone), the flush is of channel 1 where the BBC flushed its buffer 6, and the BBC's store of $12 into its sound block ($5910) is gone.
C64 addition: check_player_drain's copy of the sound selector $0C73 from before its update (written at $1958, read back at $1965 for the test against 3).

Resets enemy X's meanie bookkeeping: $0CA0+X (the meanie it made) and $0C90+X (the target it failed to make one for) to $80, its failure count $0C98+X to 0, and $0C80+X, where the next meanie search starts, to 64. Called when an enemy is placed ($1572), after it turns ($1818) and when it takes the half-visible player as its target ($17D7). The BBC routine.

Looks for a tree to turn into a meanie against enemy $90's target. Widens the arc ($0C68 = 40) and makes the enemy the viewer. Carries on from object $0C80+enemy - 1 downwards: an existing tree within 9 tiles of the target in both x ($0900) and z ($0980) whose tile the enemy can see ($1887, $14 bit 7) is recorded in $0CA0+enemy, becomes type 4 (meanie), $0CD4 gets $68 for the redraw, and C returns clear; but if a pan is under way and the tree is on screen ($1B00), the search position is moved back so this tree is tried again next time, and the turn is abandoned ($1AF9). With no objects left it adds one to the failure count $0C98+enemy, remembers the target in $0C90+enemy and returns C set. The BBC routine.

drain_target_energy's exit for a player with no energy left to take: sets $0C4E to $80, which the gameplay loop ($12A2) and the main loop ($3588) treat as the player's defeat, and abandons the enemy's turn ($1AF9).

Moves one unit of energy from the object in $0C58 to enemy $90. The player's robot ($0B): with $0C0A already 0 it goes to $1A00; otherwise the energy drops by one, the energy icons and scanner are redrawn ($9508), sound 5 plays ($3470) and C returns set. Any other object must be safe to change during a pan ($1AF4, else the turn is abandoned): a robot becomes a boulder (type 3) and the enemy's drain timer stops, a tree is deleted ($1EEF), a boulder becomes a tree ($0CD4 = $74 for the redraw); C returns clear. Every path adds one to the enemy's store $0C88+enemy; X returns the drained object. The BBC routine with the C64's icon routine and sound call.

Turns one unit of enemy $90's stored energy ($0C88+enemy) back into a tree, which is how drained energy reappears on the landscape. Nothing stored: C set. Otherwise takes a tree object ($211D, A = 2) and has $1238 put it on a random flat, empty tile lower than the lowest enemy ($0C06); failing that, C set. If a pan is under way and the tree would be on screen ($1B00), deletes it again ($1EEF) and abandons the turn ($1AF9). Otherwise takes the unit off the store and returns the tree in X (from $91) with C clear. The BBC routine, with the current object in $91 for the BBC's $01.

After a won landscape (called from $3618): adds the player's energy, as BCD ($3462), to the landscape number $0CFD/$0CFE, sets the seed generator for the new number ($33ED), generates it ($2ACC), places its enemies ($1420) and player ($1450), which runs on through make_secret_code with $0C71 bit 7 set, then draws the secret-code screen ($3282 with A = $80), prints token 5 ($8617, SECRET ENTRY CODE and LANDSCAPE) and the landscape number ($33E1). The BBC routine.

Searches objects 63 down to 0 for something the viewing enemy may drain: an existing object that is a boulder or stands on another object. For each it reads the tile under it ($2BA8, then on the C64 LDA ($5E),Y and CMP #$C0 here: $C0 and up means an object is on the tile, bits 0-5 give the top one) and accepts the top object if it is a tree or boulder whose tile the enemy can see ($1887, $14 bit 7). Returns it in $0C58 with C clear, or C set when there is none. The BBC routine but for the tile read, which its tile routine did.

Asks $1B00 about object A; if a repeated pan is under way and the object is on screen (C clear) it falls into $1AF9 and abandons the enemy's turn, otherwise it returns with C set. Called before an enemy changes an object ($173A, $1763, $1806, $1A27).

Abandons the current enemy's turn from any depth: puts back the stack pointer saved in $0C0D at $16B6 and jumps to next_enemy_turn ($16D6), whose RTS then returns straight to the gameplay loop after its call at $129F.

May object A be changed without spoiling a pan? When $0C1F bit 7 is clear (the player is not holding the same pan key after a pan) it returns C set at once. Otherwise it makes A the current object ($91; the BBC used $01), makes the player the viewer, and asks $209B whether any of the object is on screen: C clear if it is. X and Y are kept.

Carries out the action key logged in $0C61 (entry 1 of the key log), called from the gameplay loop ($12E7). H (34): hyperspace ($2156), $0C1C = 0. U (35): turns the player's robot round by flipping bit 7 of its yaw ($09C0+viewer), with music 40 ($1B84), but only if $0C51 bit 6 is set: the key checker sets it ($11EA) whenever no action key is held, and the ASL $0C51 that tests it clears it, so holding U turns once. A, Q and the create keys first follow the sights ($1C10, then $1CDD with $0C6E bit 7 clear); with no tile or platform in the sights they are refused ($1BA9). Absorb and transfer need an object on that tile (tile byte $C0 and up; the C64 reads the byte itself after $2BA8, at $1B55); transfer needs a robot: $1214 is called, the player's object $0B becomes that robot and the tower check at $1B6E follows. Absorb goes to $1B8E, create to $1BBA. Returns C clear when an object was added or removed, C set otherwise.

Anti-cracker step inside the transfer: walks down the stack of objects under the robot just entered (object flags $0100+X: bit 6 set means it stands on the object numbered in bits 0-5) and, if it meets object 63, which is always the Sentinel's tower, stores that object's type (6) in $0CE6. The secret-code display at $33C4 halves $0CE6 to get its digit-pair count, so skipping this step gives a wrong code. Falls into $1B82. Same as the BBC.

Second half of do_action_key. $1B82: after a transfer, music 25; $1B84 (also after a U-turn): plays the music in A ($888F), sets $0C63 bit 7 so the view is redrawn, returns C set. $1B8E absorb: refused once the Sentinel's slot ($0100) is empty and for the tower (type 6); for a meanie (type 4) the enemy that made it is freed first ($1BEC: $0CA0+n = $80); the object is deleted ($1EEF) and its energy added to the player's ($2136 with C clear). $1BA9: the refusal, sound 5 with its pitch byte in the C64 sound table ($AC2C) set to $AA and back to $90 (the BBC patched $591C). $1BBA create: an object of the key's type ($2120) is paid for from the player's energy ($2136 with C set) and put on the tile in the sights ($3A/$3C, $1F16), refunded if that fails; a new robot faces the player (yaw EOR $80). C64 change besides the sound table: the current object is $91 (BBC $01).

Turns the sights' position into a gaze direction from the player's robot (X = its object): yaw = $0CC6 / 8 + the robot's yaw ($09C0+X) - 10, pitch = ($0CC7 - 5) / 16 + the robot's pitch ($0140+X) + 3 + 32/256, as 16-bit angles in $3D/$3E and $3F/$40 (the pitch also in A and $74); falls into $1C54 for the vector. The view is 20 yaw units wide, so x / 8 maps 0-159 onto it. The BBC routine unchanged: the C64 keeps the BBC's sights coordinates although it shows the sights as a sprite.

Makes a Cartesian direction from the pitch ($3F/$40, also in A and $74) and yaw ($3D/$3E): with the sine and cosine of the pitch ($0E75, $1C9D), y = sin/16 into $30/$2D and cos/16 kept in $32/$33; then with those of the yaw, z = cos(pitch) x cos(yaw) into $31/$2E and x = cos(pitch) x sin(yaw) into $2F/$2C ($1C7D). Small enough for trace_gaze to step along. The BBC routine.

Multiplies cos(pitch) ($32/$33, signed) by the sine (Y = 0) or cosine (Y = 1) at $0C00/$0C02+Y, which is in sign-and-magnitude form, through $0F9E, and stores the result as the vector's x (X = 0: $2F, $2C) or z (X = 2: $31, $2E). The BBC routine.

Returns in A (high) and X (low) the sine (Y = 0) or cosine (Y = 1) held at $0C00/$0C02+Y, divided by 16 and turned from sign-and-magnitude (sign in bit 0 of the low byte) into two's complement ($1009 negates). The BBC routine.

Adds the gaze vector ($2F/$2C x, $30/$2D y, $31/$2E z: signed, whole part then fraction) to the 24-bit position ($3A/$37/$34 x, $3B/$38/$35 y, $3C/$39/$36 z), extending each component's sign into the top byte. One step of a gaze trace. The BBC routine.
Unused byte, $00, between step_along_vector and trace_gaze; the BBC original has an unused zero byte in the same place. No traced instruction refers to it.

Follows a gaze from the viewing object ($6E) in steps of the vector at $2C-$31 ($1CBB) until it meets the landscape. C clear: it lands on a tile or platform that is not the viewer's own, and $24/$26 (from $3A/$3C) hold that tile. C set: it leaves the landscape (x or z reaches 31), goes into the ground, passes beside a boulder or tower ($60 bit 6), or would look up onto a tile, which is only allowed for an enemy looking for a robot ($0C6E bit 7) or at a boulder ($0C67 bit 7). $0C56 bit 7 comes back set when the tile holds the target ($0C58), $0CDD bit 7 when a tree is seen. Starts from the viewer's position ($1ECC); each step asks $1DF9 for the height of the tile or of an object on it ($60 = $80), with a tolerance $0C of 128/256 of a tile that the tower cuts to 16. Sloping tiles are tested at $1D46. Used for the player's sights ($1B46) and enemies' sight ($18F6). The BBC routine but for the tile read at $1D66.

trace_gaze on a tile that is not flat: its corner height goes in $73 and $77 (a copy, so the corner list wraps round), then with objects ignored ($60 bit 7 cleared) it reads the other corners through $1DF9: x+1 into $76, x+1 and z+1 into $75, z+1 into $74. It then reads the tile's shape (after $2BA8 the C64 loads the byte itself, $1D66). Shapes 4 and 12, with one level edge: stepping goes on if the gaze's whole height $3B is at or above any one corner, and the gaze is blocked only when it is below all four. The other shapes go to $1D8A.

trace_gaze for the twelve shapes with two level edges: works out from the shape number which pair of edges slopes, then uses the gaze point's place in the tile (x fraction $37, inverted for two of the four pairs, against z fraction $39) to take the nearer edge of the pair from $1DF1, as the corner (0-3) it starts from.

trace_gaze's test against one sloping edge, from corner X to X+1 (heights $73+X and $74+X): the gaze point's distance along it (x or z fraction, inverted for edges 2 and 3) goes to $02, is multiplied by the edge's rise ($0D03) with the sign applied ($1007), and added to the first corner's height. A gaze ($3B/$38) below that height is blocked ($1D44); otherwise stepping goes on ($1CE8).

Edge choices for trace_gaze's slope test. For each of the four pairs of sloping edges the two edges as starting corners: 0 3 | 1 0 | 1 2 | 2 3, i.e. (0-1, 3-0), (1-2, 0-1), (1-2, 2-3), (2-3, 3-0); $1D8A takes whichever of the pair is nearer the gaze point. Corners: 0 at (x, z), 1 at (x, z+1), 2 at (x+1, z+1), 3 at (x+1, z); an edge runs from its corner to the next. The BBC's values.

Height of the tile at ($24, $26). No object on it (tile byte below $C0): A = height (high nibble), C set if the tile slopes (shape, the low nibble, non-zero). Objects and $60 bit 7 clear: walks down the stack and returns the tile's height, C clear. $60 bit 7 set (from trace_gaze): works down the stack from the top object, setting $0C56 bit 7 if it meets the target ($0C58); a boulder near the gaze point returns the height of its top (fraction in $79) and sets $0C67 bit 7; the tower near the gaze point returns its top and cuts trace_gaze's tolerance $0C to 16; a tree the gaze passes through sets $0CDD bit 7 unless it is the target, and the walk goes on down; a gaze beside a boulder or tower sets $60 bit 6. The C64 loads and tests the tile byte itself after $2BA8 (LDA ($5E),Y; CMP #$C0 at $1DFC), where the BBC's tile routine returned it with the flag. Called from trace_gaze and from $25DB.

How far a point is from the middle of its tile, for the gaze test in the routine at $1DF9. Takes the fractional x and z of the point in $37 and $39, measures each against $80 (half a tile) and returns the larger distance in A and in $74. A fraction below $80 gives its distance through EOR #$FF, one less than the true value. Called only from $1E25 (a tower counts as hit within $64) and $1E48 (a tree or boulder, within $40). Same bytes as the BBC Micro routine.

Loads object X's position into the three 24-bit coordinates (high, low, bottom byte) that the gaze and sight-line code works in: x = xObject ($0900,X) plus one half into $3A/$37/$34, y = the object's height ($0940,X high, $0A00,X low) into $3B/$38/$35, z = zObject ($0980,X) plus one half into $3C/$39/$36. The bottom bytes are cleared; the halves put the point in the middle of the tile, where objects stand. X is preserved. Called from $1CE5 and from the row trace at $2500. Same bytes as the BBC Micro routine.

Takes object X off the landscape and frees its slot. Looks up the object's tile (its x and z into $24/$26, address from $2BA8 as ($5E),Y). If the object was standing on another one (bit 6 of its flags at $0100,X), the tile byte becomes that lower object's number with bits 7 and 6 set; otherwise it becomes a bare flat tile, the object's height ($0940,X) in the top nibble and shape 0. Then $80 goes into $0100,X to mark the slot free. X is preserved. Callers: $1A3E, $1A81, $1B9E, and $2170 (a hyperspace the player cannot pay for). Same bytes as the BBC Micro routine apart from call addresses.

Puts object X on tile ($24,$26). Sets its x and z ($0900/$0980,X) and reads the tile byte: address from $2BA8, then LDA ($5E),Y / CMP #$C0 here, a test the C64 moved out of $2BA8 into its callers (the BBC routine had it inside). An empty tile takes the object at the tile's height with $E0 in $0A00,X. A tile whose top object is a boulder (type 3) or the Sentinel's tower (type 6) takes it on top: flags $0100,X = $40 + that object's number, and a height half a unit above the boulder ($80 added to its $0A00 byte) or one unit above the tower. Any other occupant: carry set, nothing placed. On success the tile byte becomes $C0 + X, the pitch $0140,X = $F5, the yaw $09C0,X = (next landscape random number from $31CA AND $F8) + $60, and carry is clear. Keeps the tile index in $1F92 meanwhile. Callers: $126B, $1469, $1565, $156F, $1BCF.
Scratch byte of place_object_on_tile ($1F16): the tile's index within its page (the Y from $2BA8), saved at $1F29 while Y serves the lower object and reloaded at $1F60. Nothing else touches it.

Puts three one-shot switches back to their defaults by zeroing them: $0C6D (bit 6 dithers the next redraw, bit 7 hides the sights first), $0C4D (bit 7 draws the object without the landscape) and $0C1E (bit 7 cuts a dither short, tested at $8797; $1219 sets it when a key action starts). It is the way out of redraw_object ($1F9F): taken at once when the object is off screen ($1FA2) and at the end ($2092).

Redraws the object in $91 after it has changed, as the viewer in $6E sees it, and puts it into the play view. The C64 reworks the BBC routine. The BBC handled an object wider than 20 character columns in two passes, each drawn into a 20-column buffer and copied to the screen, so a close object changed in two visible halves. The C64 first fills the object's whole width ($211B, up to 40 columns) of the bitmap buffer at $E000 ($1FB3), draws the first 20 columns with buffer type 2 and the rest with its extra type 3 ($2119: 160 bytes further right, $22A2), and only then dithers ($86A5, when bit 6 of $0C6D is set) and copies the whole object at once, a column at a time through $9730, into the play view at column ($211C + $94) mod 40 with $95 as the first row ($202C-$2083). Each pass turns the viewer's yaw to the object's left edge ($209A, $1F), finds the columns ($209B), sets up the buffer ($29C7), and draws either the object alone ($8533, when bit 7 of $0C4D is set: the game-over picture) or the landscape view ($2625); the yaw is restored from the copy in $211A where the BBC subtracted the turn again. When the Sentinel has won (bit 7 of $0C4E) the dither runs 40 rounds and the final copy is skipped. The sights sprite is switched off ($9A3C) around the copy and shown again ($99DC) if $0C5F says the sights are up. Callers: $12F9, $1881, $87F9.

Low byte of the address the column copier reads the bitmap buffer from: set by $992C (from $9921,Y) and advanced by $9730 as each column goes to the play view; $2096 is the high byte. The C64 keeps this variable at the BBC's address.
High byte of the buffer read address whose low byte is $2095: written by $9935 (from $991D,Y), and carried into at $973F when $9730 steps on to the next column.

Two bytes that no instruction reads or writes (searched for direct, indexed and indirect access). On the BBC Micro they held the screen address the redrawn object was copied to; the C64 redraw ($1F9F) works with a column number in $96 instead, so the variable is left over.
How many rounds the dither routine at $86A5 runs; it counts this down at $87A4. redraw_object sets 25 at $1FA6, or 40 at $2053 for the picture shown when the Sentinel has won.

Whole part of the turn redraw_object gives the viewer so that the object's left edge sits at the left of the buffer: the object's first column ($0C62) halved at $1FC7-$1FCC (the half goes into $1F), added to the viewer's yaw at $1FD8.

Works out whether any of object $91 is in view and which character columns it covers; never for the player's own object ($0B). Gets the viewer's angle to the object ($8401), takes the object's half width by type from $2112 (at least $0CD4, which it then clears) and turns it into an angle ($933D). The left edge (yaw minus that angle, doubled into columns) is the first column, 0 if it is off to the left, not visible at 40 or more; the right edge likewise, clipped to 39. Returns carry clear when visible, with the first column in $0C62, the width in $0C6A and the width capped at 20 in $0C69; carry set when not. The C64 also keeps the first column in $211C and the uncapped width in $211B for its one-go copy in redraw_object. Callers: $1B10, $1F9F.

Half the width of each object type in 1/256 of a tile, for the on-screen test at $20A9: robot $3E, sentry $46, tree $72, boulder $7A, meanie $4A, Sentinel $4E, tower $C1. Same values as the BBC Micro.

C64 addition: the buffer type for the second drawing pass of a wide object. redraw_object zeroes it before the first pass ($1FBF) and sets 3 before the second ($2026); $1FE8 copies a non-zero value into $10, so the second part is drawn 160 bytes (20 columns) further right in the bitmap buffer.
C64 addition: the viewer's yaw, saved by redraw_object at $1FD5 before it turns the viewer towards the object and put back at $2005 (the BBC subtracted the turn again instead).

C64 addition: the object's full on-screen width in character columns (1-40), stored by $2100 alongside $0C6A but never cut to 20. redraw_object fills that many columns ($1FB7) and copies that many ($2067), and the dither routine reads it at $86A5.

C64 addition: the object's first on-screen column (0-39), stored by $20DB. redraw_object adds the view's column offset $94 to it, mod 40, to find where its copy starts ($2035); unlike $0C62 it is not moved on between passes.

Finds a free object slot for a new object of type A (0 robot, 1 sentry, 2 tree, 3 boulder, 4 meanie, 5 Sentinel, 6 tower). Stores the type in $0C61, then (from $2120) searches the flags at $0100 from slot 63 down for one with bit 7 set, which marks a free slot. None free: carry set. Otherwise the slot number goes to X and $91, the type to $0A40,X, and carry is clear. It does not place the object; $1F16 or $1238 does that. Callers: $1452, $149B, $1562, $1A67, $2158.

Second way into alloc_object_slot, used when the type is already in $0C61: runs the slot search and bookkeeping from here to $2135. Called only from $1BBA, the create action, which then charges the energy at $1BC0 and places the object at $1BCF (refunding at $1BD5 if it cannot).

Adds (carry clear) or subtracts (carry set) the energy of object X's type, from the table at $214F, to the player's energy in $0C0A. A subtraction that would go below zero leaves $0C0A as it was and returns carry set; otherwise the result is kept to six bits (AND #$3F) and carry is clear. Callers: $1BA4, $1BC0, $1BD5, $216B.
Energy units of each object type, read by adjust_player_energy at $213E and $2145: robot 3, sentry 3, tree 1, boulder 2, meanie 1, Sentinel 4, tower 0. Same values as the BBC Micro.

The hyperspace. Takes a slot for a new robot ($211D with type 0) and tries to place it on a random tile, aiming below the player's height plus one ($1238, which picks coordinates through $1272); if that fails it returns carry set. The robot's 3 units are then taken from the player ($2136). If the player cannot pay, the robot is removed again ($1EEF), $0C4C = 3 (black background with stars) and $0CDE = $80, the game ending by hyperspace. Otherwise it starts the hyperspace tune ($888F with A = 0); if the player is standing on the Sentinel's tile ($0C19/$0C1A) the landscape is won ($0CDE = $C0, $0C71 = $80); then it calls $1214 and makes the new robot the player ($0B). Both outcomes end with $0C63 = $80 (the player has moved) and carry clear. Callers: $171D, $1B1F.

Draws every object on a tile, given the tile byte in A (bits 0-5 name the top object, kept in $0C6C). Counts the stack by following bit 6 of each object's flags at $0100 down to the bottom object ($0C6B = how many sit above it). A lone object is drawn directly. For a stack it compares the player's height ($0B) with that of the object being drawn: a player below it draws the rest top down; a player above it, or level with anything but the Sentinel's tower, draws bottom up, counting down from the top each time to find the next object up; level with the tower it draws top down, so the platform hides the Sentinel's feet. Objects are drawn by $8533. Reached by JMP from $2A32. Same as the BBC Micro routine.

Fills a block of character cells of the bitmap at $E000-$FF3F (the title picture itself, and in play the buffer that is copied to the view) with one of four backgrounds. A = first row, an index into the row address tables $3D83/$3DB5 (the BBC used 0 for its screen and 25 for its buffer; on the C64 both halves of those tables give the same rows of the $E000 bitmap). X = columns, Y = rows. $0C4C picks the background, whose bytes for even and odd pixel lines come from $2286 and $228A, so each cell's eight bytes alternate between the two. Rows wider than 32 columns take two passes of at most 256 bytes. C64 change: LDX #$20 now comes before SBC #$20 ($221A), so exactly 32 columns is a single pass; in the BBC order that case began a second pass with a count of 0, which the loop runs as 256 columns. None of the BBC's four calls asked for exactly 32 (they used 40, 40, 16 and at most 20); the C64 redraw asks for any width up to 40 ($1FBA). Callers: $10A1 (40 columns, 24 rows), $1FBA.

Background byte for even pixel lines, by the background number in $0C4C, read by fill_background at $2229: $00 $00 $AA $55. In C64 multicolour, two bits to a pixel, with $228A: background 0 alternates lines of colour 0 and colour 1 (the sky in play), 1 is plain colour 0, 2 alternates lines of colour 2 and colour 1, 3 is plain colour 1. The BBC's same bytes $AA/$55 for background 2 made a checkerboard of colours 3 and 0; its colour 1 byte was $0F.
Background byte for odd pixel lines, by background number 0-3, read by fill_background at $222E: $55 $00 $55 $55 (the BBC had $0F $00 $55 $0F).

Mask of a single multicolour pixel by its position 0-3 in the byte, counted from the left: $C0 $30 $0C $03 (the BBC's mode 5 masks were $88 $44 $22 $11). Read from outside this range, at $877C, $943F and $944E.
A byte of four pixels all in one colour, by colour 0-3: $00 $55 $AA $FF (BBC $00 $0F $F0 $FF). draw_polygon_spans takes a polygon's fill byte from here at $2303.
Mask of the pixels to the left of position 0-3: $00 $C0 $F0 $FC (BBC $00 $88 $CC $EE). draw_polygon_spans uses it at $235B and $23BB to keep what is already on screen left of a span's first pixel.
Mask of the pixels to the right of position 0-3: $3F $0F $03 $00 (BBC $77 $33 $11 $00). draw_polygon_spans uses it at $2368 and $2396 to keep what is right of a span's last pixel.
Mask of position 0-3 and every pixel left of it: $C0 $F0 $FC $FF (BBC $88 $CC $EE $FF). draw_polygon_spans uses it at $2361 when a span starts and ends inside one byte.

Offset added to the start of a buffer line by buffer type ($10), read at $22D4: 0 for the left row buffer, $60 (96 bytes, 12 columns) for the right row buffer, 0 for the column buffer, and $A0 (160 bytes, 20 columns) for type 3, a C64 addition used for the second half of a wide object ($2119). The C64 adds only this low byte and the carry ($22D4-$22DC).

Four zero bytes that nothing reads: high bytes for the offsets at $22A2, which the BBC Micro added from a table of its own (three entries there). The C64's draw_polygon_spans adds just a carry to the high byte ($22DC), so these are left over, grown to four entries like the table beside them.

Draws a filled polygon into the bitmap at $E000-$FF3F (the title picture itself, and in play the buffer that is copied to the view) from its outline, one pixel line at a time: line numbers run from $06 (top) down to $04, and each line's left and right pixel x are in $AD00 and $AE00 (the BBC's $5A00/$5B00, moved +$5300). Returns at once if the middle line's right end is left of its left end (the polygon faces away). $19 holds the colours, fill in bits 2-3 and edge in bits 4-5 (bit 7 of $0C7A makes the edge the fill colour); they are patched into three ORA operands ($235F, $239A, $23BF) and the fill byte comes from $2292. Lines are clipped to the buffer area ($35 and $36 its left and right, $61 its width); $2C and $2D, set to 1 at the start, change when a line runs off the right or the left of it. C64 changes: the first line's address no longer adds the BBC's screen-or-buffer offset ($55), because the C64's row table at $3D83/$3DB5 always gives rows of the $E000 bitmap, 320 bytes apart, and $22A2 has four buffer types; moving down a character row ($231C-$2329) just adds $139, without the BBC's wrap from $5300 back to its buffer's row 16. Callers: $2AB4, $2AC8.

Patched operand: low byte of ORA $3E3C,X at $235E, written at $22F6 with the colour byte so that the edge pixels of a span that starts and ends inside one byte come from the left-edge patterns at $3E00 + colours + position. The code from here to $2376 finishes that case and moves down a pixel line (INC $72 within a character, DEY for the line number); $2377 starts a line: reads its ends from $AD00/$AE00, returns once they cross, clips the right end to the buffer and keeps the pixels right of its last one.

Patched operand: low byte of ORA $3E7C,X at $2399, written at $22FB with the colour byte plus $40, so a line's right end takes its edge pixels from the right-edge patterns at $3E40 + colours + position. After it the routine stores that right-end byte and turns to the line's left end ($239E on): a line lying right of the buffer is flagged in $2C and skipped, one starting left of it begins at the buffer's edge ($2340), one whose ends share a byte goes to $2355, otherwise the pixels left of its first one are kept.

Patched operand: low byte of ORA $3E3C,X at $23BE, written at $22F3 with the colour byte, giving the left-edge pixels of a line's first byte. The code after it points $70/$71 at that byte and works out how many whole bytes lie between the two ends ($23D0-$23D4).

Patched operand: the offset of BCC at $23DA, written at $23D4 from the byte distance between the line's ends (left offset minus right offset, halved), so the branch lands inside the unrolled run of LDY #n / STA ($70),Y from $23DC to $2457 and stores the fill byte ($58) into just the whole bytes between the two ends, working from the right one back, 8 bytes apart (one character cell each). $2458 then goes back for the next line.

Works out which of the 1024 tiles the player could see from where they stand, as a bit map at $3E80-$3EFF that corner_view_angles consults at $2911. Does nothing when bit 7 of $0CDE is set (the game has ended by hyperspace). Clears the map, builds the height tables ($25C4), then from the back row forward gets each row's corner visibility ($24E2, alternating between $0180 and $01A0 with $05) and marks every tile that has a visible corner among its four, unless the tile is flat and higher than the player's height ($0940 of object $0B). Tile (x, z) is bit (x AND 3) * 2 + (z AND 1), counted from the left ($24DA), of byte $3E80 + (x AND $1C) * 4 + z / 2. Called from $35BA. Same as the BBC Micro routine.

One bit per entry, from the left: $80 $40 $20 $10 $08 $04 $02 $01. Picks a tile's bit in the visibility map: read at $24AC (inverted) and $24C1 when build_tile_visibility writes the map, at $2916 by corner_view_angles and at $3882 by the C64's cached-angle path.

For every corner of tile row $1A, x from 31 down to 0 ($18), decides whether the player can see it and stores $FF (seen) or $00 at $0180 + $05 + x. A corner within 1.5 tiles of the player counts as seen. Otherwise it takes the vector from the player's eye ($1ECC on object $0B) to the corner divided by 256 (low bytes $2F-$31, bottom bytes $2C-$2E, sign bytes $86-$88), doubles it while halving the step count in $17 until the longest component nearly fills a byte, then steps along it ($2576), checking each step against the tile-height table. Calls the sound routine $352C once per corner. The anti-cracker check at $254A sits in the middle. C64 differences: the height tables are on page $40 + z instead of $60 + z ($24E4, $2546), and the stepping loop is written out in full. Called from $2473 and $247E.

Anti-cracker check embedded in trace_row_corners, as on the BBC. Unless bit 7 of $0CCE is set, it reads the stash written on page $3F by the secret-code comparison at $14B6-$14C7 (each byte there: generated digits minus typed digits, plus the byte at $0100). It starts at $3F00 + ($0C55 + 41) (LDA $0B56,X is $0C55, because the loop above leaves X = $FF) and works down: four bytes that must each be $7F, then the byte below them, which must not be. Any failure goes to $25D8, which restarts at the title ($1017); success sets bit 7 of $0CCE so it is not checked again. On the C64 page $3F also holds the start-up code at $3F00, which the stash may overwrite once the game is running; nothing jumps back there.

Second half of trace_row_corners: steps the scaled vector $17 times from the player's eye towards the corner. C64 change: the BBC ran one loop over the three axes with indexed adds; the C64 writes the adds out in full, keeps the count in X, the x whole part in Y and the z whole part directly in $73 as the height table's page: x ($37, Y) += ($2F, $86), z ($39, $73) += ($31, $88), y ($35, $38, $3B) += ($2D, $30, $87). After each step the height $3B is compared with the highest corner of the tile underneath at ($72),Y, the $4020 table; lower means the corner is hidden (carry set). $25B0 stores $00 or $FF at $0180 + $05 + x and moves to the next corner.

Builds the two height tables the sight-line code uses, on the C64 in pages $40-$5F, memory that is also the play view's character sets (the BBC used its screen memory, $6000-$7FFF). First, for every tile corner, byte $4000 + z * 256 + x = height * 2, plus 1 if the tile anchored there is not flat (heights from $1DF9 with bit 7 of $60 clear, so objects are ignored). Then for every tile with x and z 0-30, byte $4020 + z * 256 + x = the highest of its four corners, or its height if flat. Leaves $70/$71 at $4000 and $72/$73 at $4020 for trace_row_corners. The JMP $363A at $25D8 inside it belongs to the anti-cracker check at $254A, not to this routine. Called from $246C.

Draws the landscape as the viewer in $6E sees it, into the bitmap buffer, a row of tiles at a time from the back of the landscape to the front. C64 addition at the start ($2627-$264D): ($B1 $B0) = the viewer's pitch ($0140,X) times 16 plus 2, sign-extended, and $B2 = its yaw ($09C0,X) minus 10, the values that the cached-angle path at $37F2 subtracts ($385B-$386A). Then as on the BBC: the point pointer $3C/$3D = $0C40; from the yaw, the quadrant holding the right edge of the 90-degree view ($1C, offset $1B from $27D3, $66 = quadrant * 4, $4B = quadrant - 2) and the yaw of the view's left edge within it ($20); the viewer's tile turned into that quadrant's frame ($03, $1D). For each row from 31 down to 0 it finds the part in view ($27D7) and draws it ($295D); of the viewer's own row it draws only the part to one side of the viewer, and last the tile under the viewer, stretched across the bottom of the view ($2A4B). When bit 7 of $0C1B is set it asks $1223 after each row whether the same pan key is still held and, if not, returns carry set with the drawing abandoned; carry clear when the view is complete. Callers: $10DA, $111F, $13F7, $1FFC, $35C3.

Offset by viewing quadrant 0-3, loaded at $266D and kept in $1B by draw_view_rows: 0, 1, $21, $20. $2A1A adds it to a tile's index in the two 32-byte rows of corner data, to pick the corner that carries the tile's byte as the tile is seen from that quadrant. Same values as the BBC Micro.

For tile row $26, finds the stretch of tile corners that lies in the view, starting from column $32 (the left edge found for the row before, which is usually close). It gets that corner's angles ($283D) and steps along the row with $282E and $2836, going by the on-screen flag each call returns, until it has the first and last corners in view: the left one in $32, the right one in $33. Every corner it looks at has its angles and tile byte stored in the drawing tables on the way. Callers: $26D6 and $26FE. Same as the BBC Micro routine.
Shared exit of the two row-stepping helpers after it: returns carry set when a step would leave the row of 32 corners.
Moves one corner left along the row being searched: Y = $24 - 1 and on into corner_view_angles; when $24 is already 0 it returns carry set through $282C instead.
Moves one corner right along the row being searched: Y = $24 + 1, carry set through $282C if that would be corner 32, otherwise it falls straight into corner_view_angles below.

Angles of tile corner (Y, row $26) as the viewer ($6E) sees it, for drawing. Stores, at index Y + $05, the yaw relative to the left of the view in $0BA0 (low) and $A800 (high), the pitch in $0A80 (low) and $0AE0 (high), and the tile byte in $0180 (0 when the tile has no objects and the map at $3E80 marks it unseen). Returns A and $7F = 0 if the corner is left of the drawing area ($07, $28), $80 inside it, $81 right of it ($12); Y is kept in $24 and $0F and returned, carry clear. C64 addition, its first three instructions: while the play view is up (bit 7 of $9AF6, set by $9A51) it jumps to $37F2, which reads the corner's yaw and pitch from tables the C64 keeps at $BC00-$CBFF (written around $3773-$37E1) and subtracts the viewer's current left-edge yaw and pitch ($1F/$B2, $B0/$B1) instead of working them out. The calculation from $2845, the BBC's, is used for the title and overview pictures: yaw from $9287 with the corner's offset from the viewer's tile ($03/$1D, less $0C78), distance from $937F, pitch from $933D using the tile's height or, under objects, the bottom object's height.

Draws one row of tiles in the 3D view: row $26, columns $37 up to but not including $38. The columns left of the viewer's column $03 go first, left to right; then the columns from $38-1 down to the viewer's column, right to left, so each half is drawn from its outer end inwards. Each tile goes through draw_tile_and_objects ($2A12) with its column in $25. Called from $275D and $2790. Same code as the BBC's DrawLandscapeRow.

Swaps the drawing buffer between types 0 and 1 (the BBC's left and right row buffers): A = (bit 0 of $10) EOR 1, then falls into set_draw_buffer. Only caller: draw_polygon ($2AC0), when a polygon reaches into the other half. Same as the BBC's FlipBufferType.

Sets up the drawing window for buffer type A (0, 1 or 2; kept in $10) from the three-entry tables at $29BB-$29C6: $07 = minimum yaw high byte and $12 = $07/2 EOR $80, $11 = yaw origin, $61 = width, $35 = left edge, $36 = $35+$61, and zero in the low bytes $28 and $29. The tile-angle code tests yaws against $07/$28 and $12 ($293F-$2951); get_polygon_lines adds $29/$11 to every point yaw. Callers: $1098 and $993B (A = 0), $35D2 and $9951 (A = 2; $9951 is the BBC's UseColumnBuffer, moved into the C64's $99xx code), and flip_row_buffer. Same code as the BBC's ConfigureBuffer.

Yaw origin, high byte, for buffer types 0, 1, 2: 10, 2, 12. set_draw_buffer copies it to $11; get_polygon_lines adds it to each point's yaw ($2DA7, $2DDD) before multiplying by 8 to get a pixel x. Same values as the BBC's buffersOrigin.
Left edge in pixels for buffer types 0, 1, 2: 80, 64, 96. set_draw_buffer copies it to $35 and adds the width from $29C1 to make the right edge in $36. Same values as the BBC's xBuffersLeft.
Width in pixels for buffer types 0, 1, 2: 112, 112, 64. set_draw_buffer copies it to $61, read at $2337 and $2384. Same values as the BBC's xBuffersWidth.
Minimum yaw, high byte, for buffer types 0, 1, 2: 20, 20, 8. set_draw_buffer copies it to $07 and derives the maximum in $12 from it ($07/2 EOR $80). Same values as the BBC's buffersMinYaw.

Sets up a narrow drawing window around one object being redrawn (buffer type 2). A = the object's width in character columns, from $0C69 at the only caller, $1FE5. $07/$28 = A/2 as a yaw with a fractional low byte, $12 = $07/2 EOR $80, $61 = 4*A pixels, $36 = $80 OR (2*A AND $FC), $35 = $36-$61, origin $11/$29 = $35/8 (high byte and fraction), $10 = 2. Ends in the RTS at $29F8 that draw_tile_and_objects also uses. Same code as the BBC's ConfigureObjBuffer.

Title-screen branch of draw_tile_and_objects (bit 7 of $0C4B set): the tile's entry in the view table $0180,X is 0, or $20 plus a block-pair object type 7, 8 or 9 (written by spawn_char_rows). Type 0 draws nothing; otherwise object 63 gets that type ($0A7F), the tile's column ($25 to $093F) and row ($26 to $09BF), and is drawn by $8533 (the BBC's DrawObject) with Y = 63. The tile itself is not drawn.

Draws the tile at column $25, row $26, and anything standing on it. First calls $352C, the C64's changed copy of the BBC's ProcessSound (not traced here). Index X = (($25 OR $05) + $1B) AND 63 into the view's tile table at $0180. Title screens go to draw_title_block_tile. Otherwise the entry decides: 0 = hidden, nothing drawn; $C0 and up = an object stands there: the flat tile, then the stack of objects through $21AE (the BBC's DrawObjectStack); else the low nibble is the shape: 0 flat (draw_flat_tile), 4 or 12 two triangles (draw_two_face_tile, first point from bit 0 of $4B into $45), anything else draw_sloping_tile. Called by draw_landscape_row. Same logic as the BBC's DrawTileAndObjects.

Draws a flat tile in the chequerboard pattern: X = 0 when column $25 and row $26 are both odd or both even, else X = 8; X selects entry 0 ($3C) or 8 ($00) of tile_face_colours. The X = 8 tiles pass through set_stash_offset on the way into draw_one_face_tile. Called from draw_tile_and_objects and from $27CE. Same as the BBC's DrawFlatTile.

Anti-cracker step inside draw_flat_tile, reached only for the second chequer colour (X = 8): copies the middle byte of the seed register ($0C7D, written as $0C75,X) to $0C55 (as $0C4D,X), the BBC's stashOffset, so its last value depends on the landscape. The C64 keeps the BBC's disguised readers of $0C55: $14AC LDY $0BAB,X after LDX #$AA, and $254F LDA $0B56,X. Falls into draw_one_face_tile.

Draws a tile as a single four-sided face: colours $19 = tile_face_colours,X, polygon type $3B = 0 (quadrilateral), then jumps to draw_polygon. X is 0 or 8 from draw_flat_tile, or the tile's own shape number from draw_sloping_tile. Same as the BBC's DrawOneFaceTile.

Draws a sloping tile whose shape A is not 0, 4 or 12. Y = (A - $66) AND 15 turns the shape into one relative to the direction the viewer faces ($66 = viewing quadrant times 4). If Y AND 3 = 1 the tile is one plane and goes to draw_one_face_tile. Otherwise it is two triangles: $45 = triangle_first_point,Y, and 16 is added to the shape (choosing the other half of tile_face_colours) unless (bit 2 of the shape)/4 + $4B is 2 or more. Falls into draw_two_face_tile. Same as the BBC's DrawSlopingTile.

Draws a tile as two triangles. A = shape, plus 16 for the second colour set, kept in $34. First triangle: $3B = $80, colours from tile_face_colours,A, JSR draw_polygon. Second: colours from entry (A EOR 16), bit 6 added to $3B, and falls into draw_polygon. Same as the BBC's DrawTwoFaceTile.

Draws one polygon into the current drawing buffer. The kind is in bits 7-6 of $3B: %00 a four-sided tile face, %01 an object face, %10 and %11 the first and second triangle of a tile. Buffer type 2 ($10) is one pass: get_polygon_lines, and if it returns carry clear, the filler at $22AA (the BBC's DrawPolygonLines). With type 0 or 1 it draws into that buffer, then, unless $2C,type is 1 (the polygon stays inside), calls flip_row_buffer and draws it again into the other. Called by the tile routines above and by $859F in the object drawer. Same as the BBC's DrawPolygon.

Builds the landscape's 32 x 32 grid of tile corners at $0400-$07FF from the seed sequence. 81 seed numbers go to $AD00-$AD50; only the third ($AD4E) is used again, by set_cracker_seed. $0C08 = 24 on landscape 0000 ($0C52 = 0), otherwise 14 plus a seed number from 0 to 22 ($3451). Then: process_all_tiles $80 (a seed number in every corner), smooth_landscape 0 (average runs of four), process_all_tiles 1 (scale by $0C08, clamp to 1-11), smooth_landscape $40 (level single-corner peaks and dips), get_tile_shape for every corner x, z = 30 down to 0 with the shape put in the high nibble, and process_all_tiles 2 to swap the nibbles: altitude high, shape low. Called from the title loop ($1071) and $1A9A (the next landscape after a win). When smooth_tile_strip has patched the stack, the final RTS goes to $8817 instead of the caller. Same as the BBC's GenerateLandscape.

Applies one operation, chosen by A (kept in $1C), to all 32 x 32 tile corners, z and x each from 31 down to 0: 0 = zero the byte; $80 = store the next seed number; 1 = map a raw seed byte v to an altitude: $0C08 times |v-128|, high byte, with the sign of v-128 put back (the multiply at $0D03 and sign routine at $1007), plus 6, negatives made 0, plus 1, capped at 11; 2 = swap the byte's nibbles. Returns with N set. Called by generate_landscape (A = $80, 1, 2) and draw_title_screen (A = 0). Same as the BBC's ProcessTileData.

Smooths the whole landscape twice ($15 counts 2 passes). Each pass runs smooth_tile_strip on every row (z = 31..0, A = 0) and then every column (x = 31..0, A = $80). A goes to $66 first: bit 6 clear averages, bit 6 set levels single-corner spikes. Called twice by generate_landscape. Same as the BBC's SmoothTileData.

Points ($5E) and Y at the tile byte for corner x = $24, z = $26: page $04 + (x AND 3), offset (x/4)*32 + z, so each page holds every fourth column. Differs from the BBC's GetTileData, which also loaded the byte and set carry for an object ($C0 and up): the C64 version stops at the address, and every one of its 17 call sites that wants the byte loads ($5E),Y itself, with CMP #$C0 where the flag is needed (after the calls at $1254, $1ACC, $1DF9).

Smooths one strip of 32 corners: the row at z = $26 when bit 7 of A is clear, the column at x = $24 when set; bit 6 comes from $66 and the two are kept in $1C. Copies the strip into $AD00-$AD22 with corners 0-2 repeated at the end. Bit 6 set: working down the strip, a corner higher than both neighbours drops to the higher neighbour and one lower than both rises to the lower one. Then, if bit 7 of $0C71 is clear, writes $8816 as the return address at $01FE/$01FF: the title loop calls generate_landscape with the stack reset (LDX #$FF, TXS at $1017), so that RTS lands on $8817, whose bytes $30 $3F are BMI $8858, the landscape preview (the BBC trick, re-aimed at the C64's addresses). Bit 6 clear: each corner becomes the average of itself and the next three, then set_cracker_seed. Same as the BBC's SmoothTileCorners, plus the tile loads the shorter point_at_tile needs.

Anti-cracker step at the end of the averaging pass of smooth_tile_strip (X = 32 here): copies $AD4E, the third seed number of the landscape, which is the high byte of its BCD number, into $0F3D, the operand of an LDA # at $0F3C in other code. check_cracker_seed and $18A4 read it back. Same as the BBC's SetCrackerSeed.

Last part of smooth_tile_strip: writes the 32 smoothed bytes from $AD00-$AD1F back into the row or column of tile corners they came from (bit 7 of $1C picks which), through point_at_tile. Also the landing point of the outlier pass ($2C29).

Works out the shape number of the tile anchored at corner x = $24, z = $26 from the altitudes (low nibbles, at this stage) of its four corners: this one to $73, x+1 to $76, then x+1,z+1 to $75 and x,z+1 to $74. Comparing which corners are level and which higher gives X = 0 to 15 (0 flat; 12 for the irregular cases; 8 is never produced). $24 and $26 are left as they came in. Called by generate_landscape for each corner. Same decisions as the BBC's GetTileShape, with a tile load after each point_at_tile call.

Added (mod 64) to a triangle's first corner to get its third corner, indexed by $45 (the starting corner, 0 or 1) plus 2 for the second triangle: 1, 33, -1, 31. The corner numbers index the view's point tables, where +32 is the other row. Read at $2D60. Same values as the BBC's trianglePointAdd.

Colour byte for each tile face, 32 entries. 0-15: the only or first face, by shape; 16-31: the second triangle. Bits 2-3 and 4-5 hold two colour numbers, the fill and the edge (the filler at $22E0-$22F1 copies the first over the second when bit 7 of $0C7A is set): entry 0 ($3C) is 3 and 3, one flat chequer; entry 8 ($00) is 0 and 0, the other (shape 8 never occurs). Loaded into $19 by draw_one_face_tile and draw_two_face_tile. Same values as the BBC's tileShapeColour; how the C64 filler turns the numbers into colours is not traced here.
First corner (0 or 1) for drawing a two-triangle tile, by viewer-relative shape 0-15: 1 for shapes 6, 7, 14 and 15, else 0. Read into $45 by draw_sloping_tile. Same values as the BBC's triangleStart.

Part of get_polygon_lines, entered by BMI at $2D72 for a tile drawn as two triangles. A = the rear-left corner number. For the second triangle (bit 6 of $3B) A moves diagonally (+33 mod 64) and Y = $45+2, else Y = $45. Corner list $0C40-$0C43 = A, A EOR 32, (A EOR 32) + triangle_third_point,Y mod 64, A again; then 3 edges.

Turns one polygon into left and right x-coordinates for each line of the drawing buffer. The corners are numbers in the list at ($3C); for a tile the list is $0C40-$0C44 (pointer set at $264E), filled here from corner ($25 OR $05) as a four-sided face (4 edges in $17) or through triangle_points, while an object face comes with its list ready. Each corner's yaw ($0BA0/$A800) plus the origin ($29/$11), times 8, becomes its x in $A7A0, with a high byte in $0B40 when any x needs one (bit 6 of $6C). Each edge is then traced: from its higher end down, into $AD00 (edges whose later point is higher) or $AE00 (the others) at the offset of each y, through trace_polygon_edge, or split_long_edge when a delta needs two bytes. Level edges only widen $30/$31; a polygon of nothing but level edges becomes one line. $04/$06 end as the lowest and highest line. Returns carry clear if something is to be drawn. Same as the BBC's GetPolygonLines, with its tables moved ($5500 to $A800, $54A0 to $A7A0, $5A00/$5B00 to $AD00/$AE00).

Traces one polygon edge from its start (x $41:$18, y $3E:$1A, the higher end) to its end (x $42:$39, y $3F:$16), writing an x for each line into the table whose page is in $02 ($AD left, $AE right). First it lowers $04 and raises $06 to cover the edge, clipped to the buffer's lines $52 to $51-1, and returns at once if the edge is wholly above or below. If either x has a high byte it goes to trace_wide_edge. Otherwise X = INX or DEX (opcode) by direction, $0D = |x delta|; a steep edge ($0D < $0C, the y delta) is traced here one line per step with a Bresenham-style error in A, storing every line; a shallow one goes to trace_shallow_edge. The loops are self-modified: the step opcode and the store address are written into the code. Leaves $7F = 0 once it has traced. Same as the BBC's TracePolygonEdge part 1-2.

Self-modified opcode: the x step of the steep-edge loop, INX ($E8) or DEX ($CA), written by $2F43; skip_steep_offscreen copies it to $2FCA. The STX that follows stores X at the line given by $2F60 in the page given by $2F61.

Self-modified operand, low byte of the steep loop's STX: the current line, set to the edge's start y by $2F40, lowered by $2F62 (and $2FCB, $2FD6) each line and raised once by $2FB6; reaching 0 ends the edge.

Self-modified operand, high byte of the steep loop's STX: $AD or $AE, the left or right edge table, written by $2F3D from $02. The rest of this span is the loop's count (Y), the finish at $2F6A (Y = 0 to $7F, drawn) and $2F6D.

Shallow edge (x delta >= y delta): steps x one pixel at a time and y when the error overflows. Patches the store at $2FAD (line $2FAE, page $2FAF) and the step at $2FA1. It also chooses the branch distance at $2FA5 so each line keeps its outermost x: 7 stores after every step (the last x on a line wins; left table with DEX, right table with INX), 10 only when a new line starts (the first x wins; left with INX, right with DEX). An edge starting above the buffer goes to skip_shallow_offscreen. The BBC's TracePolygonEdge part 3.
Self-modified opcode: the x step of the shallow-edge loop, DEX ($CA) or INX ($E8), written by $2F77; skip_shallow_offscreen copies it to $2FEA.

Self-modified branch offset of the BCC at $2FA4, written by $2F8C: 7 goes to the store at $2FAD on every step, 10 skips to $2FB0 unless the line changed. The snapshot holds 7 (the BBC listing assembles 10); either is overwritten before use.

Self-modified operand, low byte of the shallow loop's STX at $2FAD: the current line, set to the start y by $2F74 and lowered by $2FA8 and $2FF1 as y steps; 0 ends the edge. $2FDC raises it by one first.

Self-modified operand, high byte of the shallow loop's STX: $AD or $AE, the left or right edge table, written by $2F71. Followed by the loop's end (DEY, BNE $2FA1) and the jump to the common finish at $2F6A.

Steep edge that starts above the buffer ($3E not 0): runs the same stepping as the steep loop without storing, with the x step copied from $2F5E into $2FCA, until the line byte at $2F60 comes down through 0, then rejoins the storing loop at $2F67. The first INC balances the extra decrement. The BBC's TracePolygonEdge part 4.
Self-modified opcode: x step (INX or DEX) of the off-screen steep loop, copied from $2F5E by $2FBC.

Shallow edge that starts above the buffer: steps x without storing, with the x step copied from $2FA1 into $2FEA and the line byte $2FAE counting down, until the edge reaches the buffer; then rejoins the storing loop at $2FB0. The BBC's TracePolygonEdge part 5.
Self-modified opcode: x step (INX or DEX) of the off-screen shallow loop, copied from $2FA1 by $2FE2. The loop ends in jumps to the common finish at $2F6C and $2FB0.

Part of get_polygon_lines for an edge whose deltas do not fit in a byte (x beyond 255, or a y delta of 256 or more): halves the x delta ($75:$74, from $A7A0/$0B40) and y delta ($76:$0C) together, counting the halvings as 2^n-1 in $40, until both fit and neither low byte is $FF. Then it walks the edge in 2^n equal sections from the higher end, each traced by trace_polygon_edge, the last ending exactly on the end point (from $0E), and returns to the edge loop at $2E8C. Same as the BBC's GetPolygonLines part 6.

Traces an edge whose start or end x has a high byte (off the left or right of the 0-255 range). $0D = |x delta| (low byte), and by direction: X = INX or DEX, $76 = the low byte at which the high byte changes (0 or $FF), $74 = INC or DEC zero-page opcode for the high byte $41. A steep edge is traced from here: patches the store at $311F (line $3120 from $1A, one more if $3E is not 0; page $3121 from $02), the step $3119 and the high-byte step $3140; a shallow one goes to trace_wide_shallow. set_edge_store_op picks STX, STY or BIT for the store as the x high byte changes. Same as the BBC's TracePolygonEdge part 6-7.

Self-modified opcode: x step (INX or DEX) of the wide steep loop, written by $30F1. When X reaches $76 the high byte changes at $3140. The store at $311F that follows has its opcode chosen by set_edge_store_op: STX $8E (x on screen), STY $8C (clamped to Y = 0 or $FF), BIT $2C (nothing).
Self-modified operand, low byte of the wide steep loop's store at $311F: the current line, written by $30F9 and lowered by $3122 and $3137.

Self-modified operand, high byte of the wide steep loop's store: $AD or $AE, written by $30EE. Followed by the loop's line and pixel counting ($3122-$313F), which handles the y high byte $3E reaching 0 by refreshing the store opcode.
Self-modified opcode: INC $41 ($E6) or DEC $41 ($C6), written by $30FE, moving the edge's x high byte when X wraps in the wide steep loop; then the store opcode is chosen again.

Wide shallow edge (x delta >= y delta, x with a high byte): like trace_shallow_edge but stores on every step through the store at $317E (line $317F, page $3180) and carries the x high byte in $41 through the self-modified INC/DEC at $319A. The BBC's TracePolygonEdge part 8.
Self-modified opcode: x step (INX or DEX) of the wide shallow loop, written by $314B. The store at $317E has its opcode chosen by set_edge_store_op (STX, STY or BIT).
Self-modified operand, low byte of the wide shallow loop's store at $317E: the current line, written by $3153 and lowered by $3179 and $3191.
Self-modified operand, high byte of the wide shallow loop's store: $AD or $AE, written by $3148. Followed by the loop's pixel count in $75 and the y high byte handling.
Self-modified opcode: INC $41 or DEC $41, written by $3158, for when X wraps in the wide shallow loop; then the store opcode is chosen again and the loop resumes at $3173.

Anti-cracker trap, reached only from check_cracker_seed with carry clear: BCC next_seed, so one extra seed number is consumed and every code digit drawn after it comes from the wrong place in the sequence. Same as the BBC's CorruptSecretCode.

Chooses the store instruction of the wide-edge loops and writes its opcode to both $311F and $317E: BIT ($2C, store nothing) while the y high byte $3E is not 0; otherwise sets $7F = 0 (something will be drawn) and uses STX ($8E) when the x high byte $41 is 0, or STY ($8C) with Y = 0 when $41 is negative and Y = $FF when positive, so off-range x values are stored clamped to 0 or 255. A is kept. Same as the BBC's ModifyStoringCode (whose commentary calls Y unused; the STY it selects stores it).

Returns the next number of the landscape's pseudo-random sequence in A. The sequence is a 40-bit shift register at $0C7B-$0C7F: eight times, it shifts left one bit, feeding in bit 3 of $0C7D EOR bit 0 of $0C7F; the result is $0C7F. Y is kept (via $31F2). Callers include generate_landscape, process_all_tiles, next_seed_bcd, spawn_secret_code, $3451, and the C64 entry code at $3FA2-$3FAF, which runs it 256 times and then stores 256 more results at $0200-$02FF. Same as the BBC's GetNextSeedNumber.
next_seed's saved copy of Y (1 byte), stored at $31CA and restored at $31EB. The BBC's yStoreNextSeed.
Prints the number 0-9 in A as a digit: adds '0' and falls into print_digit. Used by print_bcd_pair. Same as the BBC's PrintNumber.

Prints the character in A, turning '0' into 'O' (so zeros show as the letter O). When bit 7 of $0C60 is set (the secret-code screen) it goes to spawn_char_3d to build the character in 3D blocks; otherwise to $AA44, the text printer. Also used by print_input_buffer. Same as the BBC's PrintDigit.

Builds a character out of 3D block objects on the landscape, for the title and the secret-code screen. A with bit 7 clear is a character: its code goes to $0C10 and OSWORD 10 (the C64's handler at $8D81 copies the 8 glyph bytes from $8000 + 8*code to $0C11-$0C18); zTile $26 = $0C4A, X = 7, then check_cracker_seed and spawn_char_rows. With bit 7 set, bits 0-4 of A set the position instead: bit 6 clear the column ($0C49), bit 6 set the row ($0C4A). X and Y are kept. Callers: print_digit, draw_title_screen, spawn_secret_code. Same as the BBC's SpawnCharacter3D part 1.

Anti-cracker check, once per character in spawn_char_3d: if $0C75 is lower than the byte set_cracker_seed put at $0F3D (the landscape's BCD high byte), calls corrupt_secret_code. Play code at $18A2-$18B5 sets $0C75 to that byte plus 1 in BCD (it adds 7 when the low digit is 9), and the reset at $114D zeroes it, so the check can only fail from landscape 0100 up. Same as the BBC's CheckCrackerSeed.

Places the glyph as block pairs, rows X = 7 down to 0 (glyph rows 6..0, then an empty row; the glyph's last row is never used), each row one tile further back ($26 up by one). Each row drops the glyph's leftmost pixel column, then takes the pixels two at a time (left in bit 1) and writes block_pair_objects,pair into the tile data at x = $0C49..+3 through point_at_tile. The $20 in those values makes the tile's high nibble 2, which the view code reads as the corner's altitude ($2906). Afterwards $0C49 moves 4 tiles right. Same as the BBC's SpawnCharacter3D part 2.

Tile value for each pair of glyph pixels (left pixel in bit 1): %00 $20 (no block), %01 $27, %10 $28, %11 $29. The low nibble becomes object 63's type in draw_title_block_tile: types 7, 8 and 9 are the three block-pair shapes. Same values as the BBC's objBlockNumber.

Draws the title screen (A bit 7 clear) or the secret-code screen (bit 7 set, after a landscape is won). Object 63, used for every block, gets yaw 128 ($09FF) and height $2E0 ($097F/$0A3F); bit 7 of $0C4B is set for the duration; process_all_tiles 0 empties the landscape. Title: the 15 bytes of title_text through spawn_char_3d, then DrawTitleView ($13AB) with A = 5, X = 1; code screen: spawn_secret_code, then A = 0, X = 3 (the C64-Wiki screenshots show the Sentinel on blue and a robot on a starry black sky). Y = 1 in both. Callers: $1024, $1079 (A = 0), $1AA5 (A = $80). Same as the BBC's DrawTitleScreen.
draw_title_screen's copy of its argument (1 byte); bit 7 set means the secret-code screen. The BBC's screenType.

The title as spawn_char_3d input, 15 bytes: $84 (column 4), $D5 (row 21), 'THE', $80 (column 0), $C7 (row 7), 'SENTINEL'. So THE stands further back and SENTINEL spans all 32 columns. Same bytes as the BBC's titleText.

Reads a number of up to A digits (4 for the landscape, 8 for the code; kept in $74) into $0CF0-$0CF7, newest digit first, spaces where nothing was typed. Calls $8642 first, which on the C64 is a bare RTS (the BBC's EnableKeyboard selected and flushed the keyboard). Keys come from $862C (OSRDCH with Escape handling). RETURN ends it at once, however many digits were typed; only 0-9 and DEL ($7F, removes the newest) are taken; a digit beyond the limit sends VDU 7, which the C64's OSWRCH ignores ($8B78-$8BAF), so there is no beep. The buffer is shown by print_input_buffer after each change. Same logic as the BBC's ReadNumber.

Shows the input buffer at the cursor: sets bit 7 of $0C0F (plain text, no drop shadow), prints the $74 characters from $0CF0+$74-1 down to $0CF0 (first typed first) through print_digit, so a 0 shows as O, then $74 backspaces (VDU 8) to return the cursor, and clears the bit. Same as the BBC's PrintInputBuffer.

Packs the eight typed characters at $0CF0-$0CF7 into four BCD bytes at $0CF0-$0CF3, lowest pair first (units in the low nibble of $0CF0). Spaces count as 0, so a short entry is read as if it had leading zeros (RETURN alone gives 0000). $0CF4-$0CF7 are left as $FF. Called after read_number at $1041 and $1069. Same as the BBC's StringToNumber.

Returns the value of the character at $0CF0,Y (a space counts as '0'), and for Y = 4 to 7 overwrites that byte with $FF after reading it. No check that it is a digit. Used by input_to_bcd. Same as the BBC's DigitToNumber.

Prints the BCD byte in A as two digits, high then low, through print_number (3D blocks when bit 7 of $0C60 is set). Used by spawn_secret_code and print_landscape_num. Same as the BBC's Print2DigitBCD.

Takes the next seed number and forces each nibble into 0-9 by subtracting 6 from a nibble of 10 or more (so 10-15 become 4-9), returning a BCD byte in A; $33B6 holds the low digit meanwhile. Used by spawn_secret_code and $14B6. Same as the BBC's GetNextSeedAsBCD.
next_seed_bcd's low digit while it builds the BCD byte (1 byte). The BBC's lowNibbleBCD.

Draws the landscape's secret code as 3D blocks: bit 7 of $0C60 on, position column 0, row 7; X = $0CE6/2 (the object type that $1B7F stores there; by the BBC's numbering 6 is the Sentinel's tower, where a won game ends, giving X = 3); takes X+1 numbers from next_seed_bcd and prints those with X below 4 through print_bcd_pair (8 digits when X starts at 3). Then $0CE6 = $FF, one more next_seed, and bit 7 of $0C60 off. Same as the BBC's SpawnSecretCode3D.

Prints the four-digit landscape number: $0CFE then $0CFD, each through print_bcd_pair. Reached from $1AAD (the code screen, by JMP) and $8869 (the landscape preview). Same as the BBC's PrintLandscapeNum.

Starts the seed sequence for the BCD landscape number in Y (high) and X (low): $0C7C = Y, $0C7B = X (after the reset at $114D-$1193 the other register bytes are 1, 0, 0), a copy in $0CFE/$0CFD, $0C52 = non-zero unless it is landscape 0000, and $0C07 = 1 + tens digit for landscapes 0000-0099, capped at 8, and 8 from 0100 up. Callers: $104A (typed number), $1A97 (next landscape), $35FD. Same as the BBC's InitialiseSeeds.

Prints one byte of token text. A byte of $C8 or more is itself a token: it is printed whole by $8617 (token number A-$C8), with Y kept across the call; any other byte goes to $AA6A, which sends it to OSWRCH as a character or VDU code. Called from the token loop at $8621, so tokens can nest. Same bytes as the BBC routine at $33DE; only the two call addresses moved.

Picks how many enemies a new landscape gets, 1 to 8. The base, kept in $74, is the thousands digit of the landscape number (high nybble of $0CFE, whose two BCD digits are the top of the number) plus 2. Each try takes a random byte from $31CA and counts the 0 bits after its top bit up to the next 1 (7 if none): the count is added to the base when the top bit is clear, and the count plus one is subtracted when it is set. A result outside 0-7 is drawn again. Returns the result plus 1 in A. Caller: $1429. The BBC routine, byte for byte, apart from the random-number call.

Returns a random number from 0 to 22 in A: takes a byte from $31CA and adds its low three bits (0-7) to its bits 3-6 (0-15), so the values 7 to 15 are the most likely. Callers: $148B (in the tree placing at $147D) and $2AE0 (in generate_landscape). Same as the BBC routine.
