Returns the player's energy ($0C0A) in A by counting up from 0 one unit at a time, so that with decimal mode on the result comes back in BCD. Its only caller, the routine at $1A87, turns decimal mode on first and adds the result to the landscape number to get the next landscape. Same as the BBC routine.

Plays sound A: points X/Y at the 8-byte sound block $AC00 + 8*A and calls OSWORD 7 through $FFF1, the C64's stand-in ($8D81) for the BBC's SOUND call. Callers: the game sounds at $12EE, $1750, $181D, $1A1F and $1BB0, and the volume, music and sound-effect code in this block. C64 change: the BBC routine also defined an envelope for the sound (OSWORD 8) and mapped the sound number to its data block through a table; here sound n is simply block n, and no envelope is set.

Handles the volume keys. Returns at once if bit 7 of $0CE4 is set, or unless the fourth key-logger slot $0CEB (filled by the key scan at $1363) holds 0 (key 7, quieter) or 1 (key 8, louder). Steps the level in volume_level ($34B9) by 8 within 0-$78, but first waits, re-reading the key, until the sound counter $0CDF is below 2; then stores the level, writes level/8 (0-15) to the SID volume register $D418, sets $0CDF to 12, plays sound 5 as a sample of the new volume and starts again, so a held key keeps stepping. Called from $12C4. C64 change: the BBC routine rewrote the amplitudes in its sound envelopes; this one sets the SID master volume.
SID master volume: the level divided by 8

The sound volume, 0 to $78 in steps of 8 (16 levels), $78 (loudest) in the image. process_volume_keys ($347D) changes it and writes it divided by 8 to $D418. As $78 it would disassemble as SEI; it is never executed.

Pauses the game when the key slot $0CEB holds 2 (the cursor left/right key): sets bit 7 of the pause flag $0C72, fills the scanner solid ($163F with A = 8), stops all three voices ($351C), and waits until $0CEB holds 3 (the cursor up/down key); the interrupt keeps scanning the keys meanwhile ($967E). Then turns the scanner sprites off ($163F with A = 0) until its next update, and clears the flag. Called from $12BE. The BBC routine with its call addresses moved; the keys come from the tables at $138D and $139C.

Plays the next note of the current tune. $0CE7 is the position in the music data at $AB50 (bit 7 set: no tune). A byte of $C8 or more sets the note length, (byte-$C8)*4, in $0C70 and moves on; $FF ends the tune ($0CE7 = $FF). Any other byte is a pitch: it goes into sound block 3's pitch ($AC1C), the length into the sound counter $0CDF, the voice number in block 3's first byte ($AC18) advances 0, 1, 2, 0, and sound 3 is played. Reached from process_sound ($352C) when the effect number is 3. C64 changes: the voices cycle 0-2 where the BBC cycled its channels 1-3, and the envelope byte is no longer rewritten before each note.

Stops all three voices: OSBYTE 21 for X = 2, 1 and 0 through $3527. Called when the main loop restarts ($357D), when the game pauses ($34CB) and before the game-over screen ($87B2). C64 change: the BBC flushed its four sound-channel buffers, numbers 7 to 4.
Stops voice 0 only (X = 0, then into $3527). Callers: $12E4 and $12FC. C64 change: the BBC flushed its buffer 4 here, the one for sound channel 0.

Stops voice X with OSBYTE 21 through $FFF4. The C64's OSBYTE ($8F78) handles this call at $8F81: it marks the voice idle and zeroes its SID control and sustain/release registers. Callers: $196E and the loop at $351E.

Keeps sound effects going; called from the game's waits and long loops ($12C1, $24ED, $26EC, $2A12, $35D5, $362A, $3714, $87A1, $880A). Does nothing while the sound counter $0CDF is non-zero (the interrupt counts it down, $9630). Otherwise acts on the effect number in $0C73: 3 plays the next note of the tune (process_music); 4, the scanner sound, plays sound 4 and sets $0CDF to 50; 6, the game-over sound, while the pitch in $0C74 is still $3C or more, puts it in sound block 6 ($AC34), plays sound 6, waits a random 1-4 counts and lowers the pitch by one. C64 changes: the game-over sound stops at pitch $3C (BBC $50) and uses a single sound block where the BBC set two; the scanner sound no longer sets its block's pitch and amplitude first.

A decoy byte that is never executed. The secret-code check reaches play_game by pushing $356C, computed from the Sentinel's object flags ($14E5-$14F1), and returning with RTS at $14F2, so someone reading from $356C sees LDA $83A9,Y instead of the real code. The BBC program has the same byte before its PlayGame.

Starts play once the landscape's secret code has been accepted (entered through the RTS at $14F2; see $356C). Sets the play palette ($8643 with A = $83), waits for a key ($8629: the PRESS ANY KEY of the landscape preview), switches the display to the play screen ($9A51 with A = $80: VIC bank 1, multicolour text, the five character sets and the matrix at $7C00), clears bit 7 of $0CFC to mark a game in progress, and runs into main_game_loop. C64 addition: the call to $9A51.

The main loop's first part, run after play_game and whenever $127C in play_loop asks for a fresh view (JMP at $3642); the cases it handles are the quit flag, the end of the game, a U-turn and a new position. Stops the voices; quits to the title ($1017) if bit 7 of $0C64 is set; restarts the landscape (at $35F4) if bit 7 of $0C4E is set (the player's energy ran out). Otherwise blanks the screen to blue ($8643 with A = 6), zeroes $55, $08, $0CC9, $0C5F and the scanner switch $0C04, turns all sprites off ($D015 = 0), and makes the player ($0B) the viewer ($6E). If bit 7 of $0CDE says a hyperspace ended the game, bit 6 set means the landscape is won (on to finish_landscape, $3603) and clear means it is lost (the screen is cleared and not redrawn). Otherwise, unless this is a U-turn (bit 7 of $0C51), it works out tile visibility ($245B) and the per-tile angles (precompute_tile_angles, $3700); then clears the screen ($1090), draws the view ($2625), the icons and the scanner ($9508), and has the picture shown ($98B2). It then sets the drawing up for buffer use ($55 = $19, $2993 with A = 2), lets any tune finish (process_sound), sets the play palette ($8643, A = $83) and goes on to play_loop ($363D), or after a lost game sets $0C4E, sound effect 6, shows the game-over screen ($87B1, A = 5), resets the variables ($114D) and restarts the same landscape (init_landscape_seed $33ED, then $106C). C64 changes: blue is colour 6 (the BBC's 4); $0C04 and $D015 are cleared directly where the BBC called a routine that also paused; the calls to $3700 and $98B2 are new.
all sprites off (sights and scanner)

Runs when a hyperspace from the Sentinel's pedestal has won the landscape. Blanks the screen to blue ($8643, A = 6), clears the sound effect ($0C73) and the upper four bytes of the random generator's register ($0C7C-$0C7F), switches to the bitmap display and resets tile visibility and the object table ($117C), works out the next landscape and shows its secret code ($1A87), sets the title palette ($8643, A = $87), starts the music ($888F with A = $42) with $0CDF = 10, waits for it to end, prints PRESS ANY KEY (token 6, $8617), waits for a key ($8629) and goes back to the title ($1017). C64 changes: blue is colour 6 (the BBC's 4), and it calls $117C, which switches to the bitmap display ($9A51, A = 0) before resetting.

The main loop's second part, where play happens. Calls $127C, which handles the game keys and returns with carry set when a fresh view is needed (then back to main_game_loop). Otherwise a pan is under way: copies the pan key $09 to $08, zeroes $0CD1 and $0C1E, sets bit 7 of $0C1B unless the sights are on ($0C5F), turns the player and draws the newly exposed part of the view ($10B7), clears $0C1B, and copies the number of scroll steps from $0CD1 to $0CC1. C64 change: the BBC now waited while its interrupt scrolled the screen $0CC1 times. Here the interrupt only sets $0CD8 to $80 while $0CC1 is non-zero ($964F-$9656), and this loop does each step itself: $96A6 (advances the scroll offsets $94-$97, moves the sights sprite with them when the sights are on, and decrements $0CC1); a delay of about 400 cycles unless the raster ($D012) is already between lines 230 and 255; JSR $B006, code missing from this copy; then the enemy timers ($130C) and the scanner ($1635), which the interrupt skips while a step is pending, unless bit 7 of $0CE5 is set; then it clears $0CD8. It repeats until $0CC1 is zero, then loops back to $127C.
bit 7 set by the interrupt ($9654) when a scroll step is due
raster line (low 8 bits): lines 230-255 skip the delay
about 400 cycles: 80 times DEX/BNE
missing from this copy: $B000-$B5FF holds only fill (orientation.md)
enemy timers and scanner, skipped by the interrupt while the step was pending

C64 addition. For every corner of the 32 x 32 tile grid, works out its yaw and pitch as seen from the middle of the viewing object's tile (object $6E; its x and z from $0900/$0980 go to $03 and $1D) and stores them in four 1 KB tables indexed like the tile data at $0400 (tile x, z at page base + (x AND 3), offset (x AND $1C)*8 + z): yaw low bytes at $BC00, yaw high at $C000, pitch low at $C400, pitch high at $C800. The yaw comes from $9287 with the x and z offsets, the distance from $937F, and the pitch from $9287 again with the height difference and that distance, shifted right four bits with its sign kept. The corner's height is the tile's own (high nybble of its data byte) or, if objects stand there, the y ($0940) of the lowest one, reached through the object flags at $0100; the viewer's y is at $0940/$0A00. Calls process_sound once per row of 32. Called only by main_game_loop ($35BD), after the visibility pass, whenever the player has a new position; tile_view_angles_fast ($37F2) reads the tables. The pointers at $A8/$AA/$AC/$AE get only their high bytes set here; their low bytes are 0 in both snapshots and no traced code writes them.
keep sound going: once per row of 32 tiles
yaw of the corner from the viewer ($8A/$8B)
horizontal distance into $7C/$7D
pitch of the corner ($8A/$8B), then shifted right 4

C64 addition: the play-screen version of the tile-angle routine at $2845, taken from $2842 when bit 7 of $9AF6 is set (the play display is on; $9A51 stores it). Same inputs: the tile in Y (stored in $24) and $26, the view quadrant in bits 7-6 of $1C, $05 (and $21 = Y OR $05 becomes the output index X). Maps the tile to the landscape square as $2845 does, but instead of computing angles it reads the ones precompute_tile_angles stored for that square and makes them relative to the view: yaw minus ($B2, $1F) into $A800,X/$0BA0,X (high/low) and pitch minus ($B1, $B0) into $0AE0,X/$0A80,X; $2625 sets $B2 to the viewer's yaw minus 10 and $B1:$B0 to the viewer's pitch shifted like the table. Copies the square's data byte to $0180,X, or 0 when it holds no object and its bit in tile_visibility ($3E80) is clear. Returns A = X = $7F: bit 7 set when the relative yaw is at least the buffer's minimum in $07/$28 (high/low), bit 0 also set when its high byte is at least the one in $12; Y restored from $0F; carry clear.
precomputed yaw, made relative to the view
precomputed pitch, made relative to the view

C64 addition. Stores A into every other byte of view rows 1 to 8 of the bitmap at $E000 ($E140-$EB3F), 32 unrolled stores, one per 80-byte quarter row, at offsets X, X-2, ... down to 0 or 1. The pan code ($10B7) calls it twice for a look up or down, X = $4F with A = $55 and X = $4E with A = $00, clearing the 8 character rows it is about to redraw to striped sky: odd pixel lines all colour 1, even lines colour 0.

C64 addition. Stores A into every other byte of the first 128 bytes (character columns 0-15) of view rows 1 to 24 of the bitmap at $E000 (24 unrolled stores, rows $E140 to $FE00), at offsets X, X-2, ... down to 0 or 1. The pan code ($10B7) calls it twice for a pan left or right, X = $7F with A = $55 and X = $7E with A = $00, clearing the 16-column strip it is about to redraw to striped sky.

Where each row of the view bitmap goes in the play screen's character sets: low bytes of the address of the row's first character, 25 entries in the order of the row tables at $3D83 (bitmap rows 1-24, then row 0); high bytes at $3A20. Entries 0-4 are rows 1-5 in the $4000 set (characters 40, 80, 120, 160, 200), 5-9 rows 6-10 in $4800 (0-160), 10-14 rows 11-15 in $5000 (200, 0, 40, 80, 120), 15-19 rows 16-20 in $5800 (160, 200, 0, 40, 80), 20-23 rows 21-24 in $6000 (120, 160, 200, 40), and 24 is row 0 at $4000 (0). Read at $8758, $9495, $975D and $97AD. C64 only; the 7 bytes after it are unused.

High bytes for row_char_addr_lo ($3A00), 25 entries: $41, $42, $43, $45, $46 for the $4000 set, $48-$4D for $4800, and so on to $40 for row 0. Read at $8762, $949C, $9765 and $97B5. C64 only; the 7 bytes after it are unused.

For each entry of $3A00: 0, or the number of pages to a second copy of the same row in the next character set ($08, or $20 for row 0, whose copies are $4000 and $6000). The doubled rows are 5, 10, 15, 20 and 0, the rows the interrupt's character-set switches at raster lines 54, 94, 134, 174 and 214 fall inside (row n spans lines 51+8n to 58+8n), so their characters must exist in both sets. Read at $876A, $94A4, $976F, $977F and $97BC. C64 only; the 7 bytes after it are unused.

The first character code of each screen row 0-24 in the play screen's matrix: 0, 40, 80, 120, 160, 200 repeating every six rows, and 40 for row 24. The matrix fill at $9AB8 produces the same pattern by counting, and no instruction in this image reads this table; the code missing at $B000-$B5FF is the only candidate. C64 only; the bytes after it, to $3AFF, are unused.

Arctangent table, low bytes: entry n (0-256) at $3B00+n is the fractional part of arctan(n/256) in the game's angle units (256 to a full turn); the whole part is at $3C01+n (0-32), so entry 256 is exactly 32, 45 degrees. Checked against the formula for every entry. Read by the angle routine at $0E22-$0E5A, which also uses entry n+1 when further bits of the ratio call for it (flags in $78). The same bytes at the same address as in the BBC program. This label is entry 0.
arctan_lo entries n = 1 to 64 ($3B01-$3B40). The angle routine also reads through this address ($0E38, $0E53) to fetch entry n+1.
arctan_lo entries n = 65 to 128 ($3B41-$3B80).
arctan_lo entries n = 129 to 192 ($3B81-$3BC0).
arctan_lo entries n = 193 to 256 ($3BC1-$3C00); the last is 0, since arctan(1) is exactly 32 units.

Arctangent table, high bytes: the whole part (0 to 32) of arctan(n/256) in angle units, entry n at $3C01+n, paired with arctan_lo at $3B00+n. The same bytes at the same address as in the BBC program. This label is entry 0.
arctan_hi entries n = 1 to 64 ($3C02-$3C41); also read through this address ($0E3F, $0E5A) as entry n+1.
arctan_hi entries n = 65 to 128 ($3C42-$3C81).
arctan_hi entries n = 129 to 192 ($3C82-$3CC1).
arctan_hi entries n = 193 to 256 ($3CC2-$3D01); the last is 32.

Half-angle tangents: entry n (0-128) is 512 * tan(arctan(n/128) / 2), rounded (0 to 212); checked against the formula for every entry. The hypotenuse routine $937F looks it up (at $9388) with the ratio of the shorter to the longer side and adds the shorter side times this factor to the longer side. The same bytes at the same address as in the BBC program. This label is n = 0-63.
tan_half_angle entries n = 64 to 128 ($3D42-$3D82).

Low bytes of the address of each character row of the view bitmap at $E000 (320 bytes a row), 25 entries in the order rows 1-24, then row 0: $E140, $E280, ... $FE00, $E000; high bytes at $3DB5. Read by the drawing code ($2235, $22D0) and by the picture copy ($98D3). C64 values: the BBC table here held rows of the BBC's screen memory.

A second copy of the bitmap row low bytes, identical to $3D83; read at $8727. On the BBC this table addressed the rows of an off-screen buffer; the C64 draws into the one bitmap at $E000, so both tables hold the same addresses.
High bytes for bitmap_row_lo: $E1, $E2, $E3, $E5 ... $FE, then $E0 for row 0. Read at $223A, $22D9 and $98D8. C64 values.
High bytes for bitmap_row_lo_copy, identical to $3DB5; read at $8730. The 25 bytes after this table ($3DE7-$3DFF) are the BBC's sights stash, unchanged and unused: the C64's sights are a sprite.

Left-edge pixel bytes for filling polygons: 16 groups of 4, chosen by the polygon colour byte, a multiple of 4 whose bits 4-5 are the edge colour and bits 2-3 the fill colour. Entry x (0-3) of a group has multicolour pixel x in the edge colour and pixels x+1 to 3 in the fill colour (pixels left of x are 0, to be kept from the screen). The drawing code patches the colour byte into the low byte of ORA $3E3C,X at $235E and $23BE ($22F3, $22F6). C64 values for two-bit pixels (pixel 0 in bits 7-6); the BBC's table here was for its own pixel layout. This label is groups 0-14.

Group 15 of edge_pixels_left, colour byte $3C (edge and fill both colour 3): $FF, $3F, $0F, $03. The operands at $235F and $23BF hold $3C in this image because $3C was the last colour byte patched in, which is why a symbol sits here.

Right-edge pixel bytes, laid out like edge_pixels_left: entry x of a group has pixels 0 to x-1 in the fill colour, pixel x in the edge colour and pixels right of x 0. Reached through ORA $3E7C,X at $2399, whose operand low byte is the colour byte OR $40 ($22F9-$22FB). C64 values. This label is groups 0-14.
Group 15 of edge_pixels_right, colour byte $3C: $C0, $F0, $FC, $FF. The operand at $239A holds $7C in this image, hence the symbol.

One bit per tile, set when the tile can be seen from the player's position. Tile (x, z) is bit $80 >> ((x AND 3)*2 + (z AND 1)) of byte $3E80 + (x DIV 4)*16 + z DIV 2, so this half holds x = 0-15. Built by the visibility pass $245B (cleared at $2466, bits set at $24CF), set to all $FF by $1185 and cleared by $1404; read at $24C8, $2911 and $387D. Working data, $FF throughout in the hand-over image; at the same address as in the BBC program.
Second half of tile_visibility: the tiles with x = 16-31 (also set to $FF at $1188).

The game's entry, run once. Calls the machine set-up ($8900), sets bit 7 of $0CFC (no game in progress), points the IRQ vector at the play interrupt $95E9, clears the four sprite shapes at $7000-$70FF, sets the sprite pointers ($7FF8-$7FFB = $C0-$C3: shapes at $7000, $7040, $7080, $70C0), draws the sights cross into sprite 0's shape, turns multicolour on for sprites 0-3, puts sprites 1-3 side by side at the top right (x = 264, 288, 312; y = 51) in white for the scanner and sprite 0 at y = 154, sets the five bytes of the random generator's register $0C7B-$0C7F to 1, runs the generator ($31CA) 256 times, stores its next 256 bytes at $0200-$02FF (the scanner's specks, read at $1670), and jumps to the title loop ($1017). All C64: the BBC program has its own machine set-up at $3F04. Once a landscape is generated, $14C7 writes the secret-code stash from $3F00 up over this spent code (checked by the code around $255B); in the play snapshot $3F8D-$3FB7 differ.
IRQ vector to the play interrupt $95E9
sights cross, vertical bar: alternate rows $20 and $10
sights cross, horizontal bar in row 5
sprites 1-3: x bit 8 set (x = 264, 288, 312)
256 random bytes for the scanner's specks
Characters $F0-$F9 of the first view character set ($4000): the icon and scanner-frame glyphs of the top row, copied from $ABB0 into all five sets by $98E8-$98FD.
Characters $F0-$F9 of the $4800 set: the icon glyphs (copied by $98F0).
Characters $F0-$F9 of the $5000 set: the icon glyphs (copied by $98F3).
Characters $F0-$F9 of the $5800 set: the icon glyphs (copied by $98F6).
Characters $F0-$F9 of the $6000 set: the icon glyphs (copied by $98F9).

Sprite 0's shape (pointer $C0), the sights: a cross 11 lines high whose vertical bar is the middle byte of rows 0-10 ($20 and $10 alternately, one multicolour pixel in the sprite's own colour, then in multicolour 0) and whose horizontal bar is row 5 ($99 $99 $98, the two colours alternating across 11 pixels); with the colours $98FF-$9909 sets (white and black) it shows on any ground. The entry clears $7000-$70FF and writes the cross ($3F13-$3F5F); $99DC places and shows the sprite, $9A3C hides it. This label is row 0's left byte (0).
Sights sprite, row 0: the middle byte, $20, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F33); then row 0's right byte and row 1's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 1: the middle byte, $10, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F47); then row 1's right byte and row 2's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 2: the middle byte, $20, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F36); then row 2's right byte and row 3's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 3: the middle byte, $10, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F4A); then row 3's right byte and row 4's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 4: the middle byte, $20, the vertical bar just above the crossing (written at $3F39); then row 4's right byte, 0.
Sights sprite, row 5 (the horizontal bar), left byte: $99, pixels in the sprite's colour and multicolour 0 alternately (written at $3F55).
Sights sprite, row 5, middle byte: $99, the centre of the cross (written at $3F5A).
Sights sprite, row 5, right byte: $98, the horizontal bar's last three pixels and an empty one (written at $3F5F); then row 6's left byte, 0.
Sights sprite, row 6: the middle byte, $20, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F3C); then row 6's right byte and row 7's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 7: the middle byte, $10, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F4D); then row 7's right byte and row 8's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 8: the middle byte, $20, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F3F); then row 8's right byte and row 9's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 9: the middle byte, $10, part of the vertical bar (written at $3F50); then row 9's right byte and row 10's left byte, both 0.
Sights sprite, row 10: the middle byte, $20, the bottom of the vertical bar (written at $3F42); after it row 10's right byte, rows 11-20 and the shape's unused 64th byte ($7020-$703F), all 0.

Sprite 1's shape (pointer $C1), the left part of the scanner at the top right (x = 264, y = 51). Cleared by the entry; the scanner update ($1635-$169D) writes speck bytes, chosen from its patterns at $16A1 by the random bytes at $0200, into rows 0-3 ($7040-$704B); the rest stays 0.
Sprite 2's shape (pointer $C2), the middle part of the scanner (x = 288): rows 0-3 ($7080-$708B) get speck bytes from the scanner update at $1635; the rest stays 0.

Sprite 3's shape (pointer $C3), the right part of the scanner (x = 312): only the first two bytes of rows 0-3 get specks, so the scanner is 8 bytes (64 screen pixels) wide and 4 lines high across the three sprites, inside the frame characters at columns 29-38 of the icon row. The rest stays 0.

The play screen's matrix (VIC bank 1, $D018 = $F0). $9AB8 fills it: characters 0-239 in order, four times, then 40-79 for row 24; row 0 then holds the icon characters $F0-$F9, written at $9580 (and set to $F0 throughout by $87BE).
Sprite 0 pointer: $C0, the sights shape at $7000 (set at $3F1F).
Sprite 1 pointer: $C1, scanner shape at $7040 (set at $3F24).
Sprite 2 pointer: $C2, scanner shape at $7080 (set at $3F29).
Sprite 3 pointer: $C3, scanner shape at $70C0 (set at $3F2E).

The text font: the BBC Micro's own 8 x 8 characters, character n at $8000 + 8n for n = $20 to $7E. OSWRCH computes the address at $8BDC-$8BEC; codes below $20 are VDU controls and $7F a delete, so $8000-$80FF and the $7F slot at $83F8 are never drawn. $8100-$813F: space ! " # $ % & '.
Font characters $28-$2F: ( ) * + , - . /.
Font characters $30-$37: the digits 0 to 7.
Font characters $38-$3F: 8 9 : ; < = > ?.
Font characters $40-$47: @ A B C D E F G.
Font characters $48-$4F: H I J K L M N O.
Font characters $50-$57: P Q R S T U V W.
Font characters $58-$5C: X Y Z [ \ (to $82E7).
Font characters $5D and $5E: at start $89C5 replaces the ']' glyph with a right-pointing arrow (00 08 04 3E 04 08 00 00); '^' is unchanged. Where the game prints the arrow was not found.
Font character $5F: at start $89C5 replaces '_' with a short dash across the middle of the cell (row 3 = $7C).
Font characters $60-$67: the pound sign (the BBC Micro's character $60) and a b c d e f g.
Font characters $68-$6F: h i j k l m n o.
Font characters $70-$77: p q r s t u v w.
Font characters $78-$7A: x y z (to $83D7).
Font character $7B: at start $89C5 replaces '{' with a pattern of 4-pixel blocks, rows F0 F0 0F 0F 0F F0 F0 00.
Font characters $7C-$7F: at start $89C5 replaces '|' with the blocks F0 F0 00 00 00 F0 F0 00; then '}', '~', and the $7F slot, which OSWRCH never draws.
A lone RTS that nothing calls or jumps to; the BBC program has the same unused byte just before its GetObjectAngles (at $5C00 there, this block's BBC address).

Measures object Y as seen from the viewing object $6E: records its number ($6F) and type ($0A40,Y into $4C), gets the x/z and height offsets between them ($85C4, $85F5) and the direction to it ($9287), then stores the yaw relative to the left edge of the view (direction minus the viewer's yaw $09C0,X and $1F, plus 10) in $0C57/$0C59, the object's own facing relative to that direction in $5A/$59, the distance ($937F) in $0C5D/$0C5E and the height offset in $0C5B/$0C5C. When $141F is 0 (the landscape preview) the object is turned to face the viewer ($5A/$59 = $80/$00) and drawn at double size by halving its distance and height offset (and adding $70 to the height's low byte). Callers: $189F, $20A1, $8533. The BBC routine (+$2800) with one C64 change: the test for object #63, the Sentinel's tower, now comes before the turn, so in the preview the tower keeps its own facing; the BBC turned it too and only skipped the doubling.
C64: tower test first; the BBC set $5A/$59 before it

For each point of the shape of the object measured by get_object_angles (type in $4C; its point range from $9CA0/$9CA1), works out the point's view-relative yaw and pitch: turns the point (its yaw $9DE0,Y plus the object's facing $5A/$59, and its distance $A060,Y) with the sine and cosine from $0F70 and the multiply at $0D03, adds the result to the object's distance and height ($0C5D/$0C5E, $0C5B/$0C5C; point heights at $9F20,Y), gets the yaw ($9287) and pitch ($933D), and stores them from index $40 up: yaw plus the object's view yaw ($0C57/$0C59) in $A800/$0BA0, pitch in $0AE0/$0A80. Called from $853D. The BBC routine with only addresses moved: shape tables +$5300 (BBC $49A0 is $9CA0 here), the yaw high-byte table $5500 is $A800.

Draws object Y in the 3D view. $8401 (the BBC's GetObjectAngles) works out the object's bearing and distance from the viewer; bit 7 of $0C7A is set when the distance high byte ($7D) is 15 or more (on the BBC the flag that draws a distant object's polygon edges in its fill colour), and cleared again at the end; $8475 (the BBC's GetObjPointAngles) projects every point of the shape. The object's type ($4C) gives its polygon numbers, from $9CAB,X up to $9CAC,X; each is drawn by $2AA9 with its colour bits (bits 2-5 of $A1A0,Y into $19), its side count (bits 0-1 plus 3 into $17) and its point list ($A2E0/$A420 into $3C/$3D). Types with a non-zero entry at $9CB6 can be drawn in two passes, bit 7 of each polygon's $A1A0 byte choosing its pass ($0C47). Ends with $3C/$3D = $0C40, Y restored from $6F. Byte for byte the BBC's DrawObject ($5D33), the tables moved +$5300 and the polygon routine to $2AA9.

Ground-plane vector from object X to object Y, for $8401 (its only caller): $86 = x of Y minus x of X ($0900) minus the offset in $0C78, $83 its size; $88 = z of Y minus z of X ($0980), $85 its size; the low bytes $80 and $82 are zeroed. Same bytes as the BBC's GetHorizontalDelta ($5DC4).
Height of object Y above object X for $8401 (its only caller): $81 = low bytes ($0A00) subtracted, $84 = high bytes ($0940) with the borrow. Same bytes as the BBC's GetVerticalDelta ($5DF5).

C64 only. Fills the 320 bytes $E000-$E13F, the first 40-cell row of the bitmap-layout area at $E000, with $55 (colour 1 in all four pixels of every byte); the screen buffer's row 0 starts right after it at $E140 ($3D9C/$3DCE). Its one caller, $1093 in the screen-clearing routine at $1090, stands where the BBC calls ClearIconsScanner.

Prints text token X: takes the token's start from $AA84,X and passes each byte from $AA96 plus that offset, up to the $FF that ends it, to $3414, which prints it or, for bytes $C8 and up, prints token byte-$C8 by calling back here (saving Y round the call). The BBC's PrintTextToken ($36AD), moved here with its tables at $AA84/$AA96. Callers include the title loop ($1029-$1083), $1AAA, $3420, $3634 and $8866.

Waits for a key and returns its ASCII code in A: $8642 (nothing on the C64) then $862C. The BBC's ReadKeyboard ($5E07), which re-selects and flushes the keyboard first. Callers: $1031 and $1086 in the title loop and $3637.

Reads a key through OSRDCH ($FFE0, the C64's $8D2C) and returns it in A. The code after the BCC is the BBC's Escape handling (carry set and A = $1B: acknowledge with OSBYTE $7E, read again); the C64's OSRDCH always returns carry clear, so $8631-$863E never runs, and OSBYTE $7E would do nothing anyway. Same bytes as the BBC's ReadCharacter ($5E0A). The number entry calls it directly at $32E9.

Just an RTS where the BBC's EnableKeyboard (OSBYTE 2 to take input from the keyboard, then a flush of the keyboard buffer) was: the C64's OSRDCH reads the matrix itself and has no buffer to flush. Called from $8629 and from the number entry at $32D7.

Sets the four display colours. A with bit 7 clear: C64 colour A for all four (callers pass 6, blue, to blank the screen; the BBC passes its blue, 4). A with bit 7 set: logical colour n gets entry (A AND $7F) - 3 + n of $869D ($83 and $87 are used). Colour 0 goes to $D021; colour 2 to $D023 and $869C; colour 1 to $D022 and, packed with colour 2 as high and low nybble, to all of $CC00-$CFFF (the title bitmap's screen matrix); colour 3 to colour RAM through $9AE4, with bit 3 (multicolour cell) added while bit 7 of $9AF6 marks the play screen. So a logical colour is the same bit pair on the title's multicolour bitmap and on the play screen's multicolour characters. The BBC version sends VDU 19 per colour; this one writes the VIC and the matrix itself.
Logical colour 2 as $8643 last set it ($8661), kept so the colour-1 pass can pack colours 1 and 2 into each byte of the title's screen matrix ($8682). C64 only; 2 (red) in the image.

Two palettes for $8643, four C64 colours each, logical colour 0 first. $869D-$86A0, used with $83: blue, black, then the two colours $1446/$144C write per landscape; $86A1-$86A4, used with $87: 6 blue, 0 black, 2 red, 7 yellow. They are the BBC's colourPalettes (4, 0, 6, 3 and 4, 0, 1, 3) in C64 colour numbers.
Logical colour 2 of the play palette ($83): rewritten for each landscape by $144C from the table at $14F3, indexed by the number of enemies less one ($0C6F). 3 (cyan) in the image.

Logical colour 3 of the play palette ($83): rewritten for each landscape by $1446 from $14D4, by the number of enemies less one; 7 (yellow) in the image. The next four bytes are the $87 palette: 6, 0, 2, 7 (blue, black, red, yellow).

Copies the view from the screen buffer ($E140 onwards, rows at $3D9C/$3DCE) to the play screen's character sets a random pixel pair at a time, so the new picture dissolves in. Width: the column count in $211B (the BBC uses bufferColumns x 8 bytes), with a covering bit mask from $15C4 in $0CCF. Each step multiplies a private 24-bit random number ($87B0, $A3, $A4) by 5 (the BBC calls GetRandomNumber under SEI) and takes from it a column ($9D, below $211B), a character row ($9E, 0-23), a byte pair in the cell ($9F and $9F+4) and a pixel (0-3, mirrored in the second byte, masks $228E and $9500). The target is screen row ($9E+$97) mod 25 through $3A00/$3A20 and column ($9D+$96) mod 40, written again $3A40,row pages higher. With bit 7 of $0C1E set it returns after one step; otherwise 96 steps (the BBC: about 256 of one pixel), then $352C for the sound, until the count in $2099 runs out. Called from $2056.

Low byte of the dither's own 24-bit random number (middle byte $A3, high $A4): $86C1-$86ED multiply it by 5 at every step. Nothing else reads or writes the three bytes: unlike the BBC, the dissolve does not draw on the main random number routine at $93AE. C64 only.

Ends a game; A = the number of decay passes to run first. Silences the three voices ($351C), turns the sprites off ($D015), points the 40 cells of the play screen's top row ($7C00-$7C27) at character $F0 (where the BBC calls ClearIconsScanner), starts the game-over sound ($0C73 = 6, pitch $0C74 from $E6; the BBC starts at $FA), decays the screen ($8801), then sets up the object of the type in $0C1C for the game-over view ($8819, configuration 0), sets the background ($0C4C = 3) and drawing flags ($0C4D, $0C6D, $0C1E), starts tune $32 ($888F), draws it ($1F9F) and decays for 30 more passes. Called from $12A9 and $35F1. The BBC's ShowGameOverScreen, except that the current-object variable is $91, not $01 as on the BBC ($87E7): on the C64 $00 and $01 are the processor port.

A passes of 30 ticks each; a tick is $945F (the C64's random-dot plotter, 27 rounds a call) then $352C (sound). The BBC's DecayScreenToBlack, which calls DrawBlackDots and ProcessSound at the same points. Called twice by $87B1.

A $4C (JMP) byte that is never executed: $8816-$8818 read as JMP $3F30. The landscape generator puts $8816 on the stack as a return address ($2C1E-$2C28: LDA #$88 / LDA #$16 into $0100,X), and an RTS resumes one byte on, at $8817. Kept from the BBC original's trap for crackers (its JumpToPreview).
Where that planted return address lands: BMI $8858, the landscape preview. Nothing jumps or branches here; if N were clear it would run on into $8819.

Sets up object 1 as a title-screen object of type A ($0A41), seen from object 2, in configuration Y (0 game over, 1 the object on top of the tower, 2 the tower): object 1's z = object 2's z plus $8855,Y, its y high byte = object 2's plus $8875,Y, its x = object 2's, its yaw ($09C1) = $8878,Y; object 2's pitch ($0142) = $8872,Y and yaw ($09C2) = $887B,Y; both y low bytes 0; the viewing object ($6E) = 2. Same bytes as the BBC's SpawnTitleObject ($5F80).
For $8819, by configuration: how far in front of the viewer object 1 stands, 5 (game over), 7, 7.

The landscape seen from above before play. $1420 (the BBC's SpawnEnemies; it also sets the play palette's colours 2 and 3 by the number of enemies), $13AB draws the view (X = 3, Y = 0, A = $80), token 4 prints PRESS ANY KEY and LANDSCAPE, $33E1 the landscape number, then $1450 (the BBC's SpawnPlayer, which goes on to check the secret code and start play); if that returns, JMP $1074 prints WRONG SECRET CODE (token 3). Reached only through the BMI at $8817. The BBC's PreviewLandscape with its calls moved.
For $8819, by configuration: the viewer's pitch, -12, -5, -5 ($F4, $FB, $FB).
For $8819, by configuration: object 1's height above the viewer in whole units, 0, 1, 0.
For $8819, by configuration: object 1's yaw, $80, $8E, $CE (128, -114, -50).
For $8819, by configuration: the viewer's yaw, 0, -8, -8.

Draws the two title-screen objects: type A on top of the tower (configuration 1) through $8887, then type 6 (the tower, in the BBC's numbering) with configuration 2 by falling into $8887. Called from $13EC. Same bytes as the BBC's DrawTitleObjects.
Sets up object 1 as type A in configuration Y ($8819) and draws it ($8533 with Y = 1).

Starts a tune: A = the offset of its first note in the music data at $AB50 (into $0CE7) and sound mode 3 ($0C73) so that $352C plays it note by note. The C64 adds $AC18 = 1: $AC18 is the voice byte of sound 3 (the music note), which $3504 steps before each note, so a tune starts on voice 2 and rotates through all three. Called from $1B84, $2181, $3627, $87F6.
Unused, to $88FF: $FF $FF $00 $00 repeated, with one $BF at $88FC, the same kind of fill as other gaps ($94D1, $9AF8). No instruction in the traced code can reach it.

C64 start-up, called once from the entry at $3F00. Masks interrupts; $00 = $2F, $01 = $35 (RAM everywhere, I/O at $D000); NMI vector $FFFA = $8F98, IRQ vector $FFFE = $8F9E; and six JMPs at the BBC operating system's addresses: $FFC2 to $8ED1 and $FFC5 to $8F0C (the BBC's GSINIT and GSREAD slots, used here for the sound's frame tick and pitch envelopes), $FFE0 OSRDCH to $8D2C, $FFEE OSWRCH to $8A6B, $FFF1 OSWORD to $8D81, $FFF4 OSBYTE to $8F78. Then the raster interrupt on ($D01A = 1) with its flags cleared, CIA interrupts off ($DC0D, $DD0D = $7F), a second store to $D019, of $64 (the title set-up at $9A7B puts the same $64 in $D012), $D011 = $1B, $D016 = $D8 (multicolour), sprites off and unexpanded, CLI, then $89C5, $8A22, $8A36, $8A03, and the SID: control 8 on all three voices, filter $D415-$D417 cleared, volume 15. Also sets $D025 = 0.

Copies four new glyphs from $89E3 over the BBC font: character $5D (']') becomes a right arrow, $5F ('_') a dash at mid height, $7B ('{') and $7C ('|') patterns of four-pixel blocks. Called only by $8900. What prints them was not found (no immediate load of these codes and none in the token text).
Glyph for character $5D, copied to $82E8: a right-pointing arrow, rows $00 $08 $04 $3E $04 $08 $00 $00.
Glyph for character $5F, copied to $82F8: a five-pixel dash on row 3 ($7C), the rest empty.
Glyph for character $7B, copied to $83D8: left half set in rows 0-1 and 5-6, right half in rows 2-4 ($F0 $F0 $0F $0F $0F $F0 $F0 $00).
Glyph for character $7C, copied to $83E0: left half set in rows 0-1 and 5-6, rows 2-4 and 7 empty ($F0 $F0 $00 $00 $00 $F0 $F0 $00).

Border black ($D020 = 0), then with interrupts masked VIC bank 1 ($DD02 bits 0-1 made outputs, $DD00 bits 0-1 = %10: $4000-$7FFF) and $D018 = $78 (screen matrix $5C00, characters $6000). Called only by $8900; $9A51 later picks the title's or the play screen's bank.
Fills colour RAM $D800-$DBFF with $0D: in the multicolour character mode set at start-up, a multicolour cell whose %11 pixels are colour 5 (green). Called only by $8900.

$D021 = 6 (blue), $D022 = 0 (black), $D023 = 1 (white), then fills $5800-$5FFF so that each byte holds the low byte of its own address: the screen matrix at $5C00 that $8A03 selects then shows characters 0-255 in order, four times over. Called only by $8900.
An RTS after the one that ends $8A36; no instruction in the traced code can reach it.

The four logical colours as fill bytes, one bit pair repeated: $00, $55, $AA, $FF. COLOUR and GCOL look their colour number up here (AND $7F, not checked against 3: 4 and up would read $8A69 onwards).
The VDU code still collecting parameter bytes, $11, $12, $19 or $1F, or 0 for none: set at $8B23, cleared at $8B0B.
Parameter bytes received so far for the code in $8A69: zeroed at $8B28, counted up at $8A7F before each is handled.

OSWRCH, reached through the JMP at $FFEE: the C64's stand-in for the BBC's VDU drivers. Keeps A, X and Y in $8CEB-$8CED (restored at $8C85), sends a byte that belongs to a pending code to $8A7F and a new one to $8B13. Text goes on the multicolour bitmap at $E000 (the title screens) in the BBC font at $8100, each character 8 x 8 multicolour pixels and so two cells wide: 20 to a row, 25 rows. There is no graphics cursor: VDU 5 text also goes at the text cursor, and a PLOT only lowers the next characters for the drop shadow. Codes that do something: 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 13, 17, 18, 25, 31, 127 and 32-126; the bell (7) the number entry sends at $331B is silent.

A parameter byte for the code in $8A69, counted in $8A6A. PLOT keeps only its fifth byte (y high) in $8CB5; TAB stores its first as column x 2 in $8CE5 and its second as the row in $8CE6, neither checked (a row of 25 or more would draw past $FF3F); GCOL skips its first and sets a graphics colour from its second, below 128 the foreground $8CB3, else the background $8CB4; COLOUR sets the text background $8CB2 from its byte, bit 7 dropped, so there is no way to set the text foreground. The current pair $8CE3/$8CE4 follows when its mode ($8CAF) is in use. The code is cleared at $8B0B after its last byte.

A byte with nothing pending: $11, $12, $19 and $1F start collecting parameters; 9 moves two cells right (wrapping to column 0 of the same row), 8 two cells left (to column 38 of the row above, row 24 above the top), 10 a row down, 13 to column 0; 4 and 5 switch to the text or graphics colour pair, 5 also setting $8CB0 so the picture shows through a glyph's clear pixels; 127 is backspace, an opaque space, backspace (A comes back as 8); other codes below 32 and all from 128 are ignored; 32-126 are drawn at $8BDC.

Draws character A (32-126): the glyph at $8000 + 8 x A into $F0/$F1, the bitmap cell $E000 + 8 x (row x 40 + column) into $F4/$F5 (a matrix address $CC00 + row x 40 + column is also put in $F2/$F3 and never used), then each glyph row's left four pixels into that cell and the right four into the next through $8CB6, one pixel row lower (rows 0-6 only) while bit 7 of $8CB5 is set. The cursor moves two cells right, to the next row after column 38.
Text cursor one row down ($8CE6), from row 24 back to row 0. Used for code 10 and when a character passes the end of a row.
Four glyph pixels to a bitmap mask: entry n has each bit of n doubled into a bit pair ($00, $03, $0C, $0F, $30 ... $FF), the multicolour pixels that a nybble of a glyph row sets.
4 or 5, the last of VDU 4 and VDU 5 ($8B80, $8B9B): which colour pair ($8CB1/$8CB2 or $8CB3/$8CB4) is in use. 4 in the image.
$00 after VDU 4, $FF after VDU 5: ANDed with the old bitmap byte where a glyph is clear, so VDU 5 text keeps the picture behind it. The delete code zeroes it round its erasing space ($8BBB-$8BCA).
Text foreground fill, $FF (colour 3). Nothing writes it; VDU 4 copies it to $8CE3.
Text background fill, set by COLOUR ($8AFE) and copied to $8CE4 by VDU 4. $55 (colour 1) in the image.
Graphics foreground fill, set by GCOL with a colour below 128 ($8AE1), used by VDU 5 text. $AA in the image.
Graphics background fill, set by GCOL with a colour of 128 and up ($8ACE), used by VDU 5 text. $00 in the image.
The fifth byte of the last PLOT (its y high byte). Bit 7 set, as after the shadow's move of -4, draws characters one pixel row lower ($8C3E, $8C62).

Writes one bitmap byte of a character: X = four glyph pixels (a nybble), Y = the pixel row in the cell at ($F4). Pixels the glyph sets take the foreground fill $8CE3, clear ones the background fill $8CE4 ORed with the old byte ANDed with $8CB0. Work bytes $8CEE, $8CE8, $8CE7.
Low byte of the cell number row x 40 + column, then shifted three times into the low byte of the bitmap offset ($8C12-$8C37).
High byte of the cell number row x 40 + column, the start of the bitmap offset's high byte ($8C1C, $8C23).
Fill used for the pixels a glyph sets: from $8CB1 after VDU 4, $8CB3 after VDU 5, or from a GCOL or COLOUR for the pair in use.
Fill used for the pixels a glyph leaves clear: from $8CB2 after VDU 4, $8CB4 after VDU 5, or a GCOL or COLOUR for the pair in use.
Text cursor column in C64 cells, 0-38 in steps of two (TAB x stores 2x).
Text cursor row, 0-24 (TAB stores its y without a check).
Shared work byte: row x 5, then x 40, in the character drawer ($8BF7); the combined pixels in $8CB6; the key number being tried in OSRDCH ($8D54).
Shared work byte: the high byte of row x 40 ($8C08) and the inverted glyph mask in $8CB6. The two bytes after it, $8CE9 and $8CEA, are not used.
The byte OSWRCH was given (its A), read back by the code handlers and returned in A.
X on entry to OSWRCH or OSRDCH, restored on the way out.
Y on entry to OSWRCH or OSRDCH, restored on the way out.
The current nybble's pixel mask from $8C9F, for $8CB6.
$00 while either SHIFT key is down, $40 when not, added to the key number in OSRDCH ($8D72), so an unshifted key reads the second table ($8FF3).
The key number OSRDCH returned last; before scanning again it waits for that key to be let go ($8D32). $08 (RETURN) in the image.

BBC Micro colour n as a C64 colour: 0 black, 2 red, 5 green, 7 yellow, 6 blue, 4 purple, 3 cyan, 1 white. No instruction in the traced code reads it; the palettes at $869D and the colour tables at $14D4 and $14F3 hold colours already translated this way.

Tests one key: X = key number, row + 8 x column (row: the $DC00 line driven low, bit X AND 7 of $8D24; column: the $DC01 bit read, X / 8), so $29 is S and $27 SPACE. Returns X = $FF with N set if the key is down, X = 0 with N clear if not; Y is lost. Sets $DC02/$DC03 for output and input and masks interrupts during the scan. Used by OSRDCH and by OSBYTE $81, which is how the game tests its keys ($0F62).
One bit per matrix line, $01 up to $80, for $8CF9.

OSRDCH, reached through the JMP at $FFE0: waits for a key and returns its ASCII code in A, carry always clear (no Escape). First waits for the key returned last ($8CF0) to be let go, then notes SHIFT (keys $39 and $26: $8CEF = 0 if one is down, else $40) and tries keys $3F down to 0, skipping the two SHIFTs, until one is down; the code is $8FB3 + key + $8CEF. Keys with no code there (function keys, cursor keys, CTRL, C=, RUN/STOP, left arrow) return 0. X and Y are kept.

OSWORD, reached through the JMP at $FFF1. Two calls exist. A = $0A copies the 8 bytes of a glyph from the font at $8000 + 8 x code into the 8 bytes after the code in the block at X (low) and Y (high), as the BBC call does; the title's large letters use it ($3225). A = $07 plays a sound ($8DB4). Any other A returns at once.

OSWORD 7, the C64's own sound block (not the BBC's), 8 bytes at XY; $3470 passes $AC00 + 8 x sound. Byte 0: voice 0-2 (SID offset from $8EBB). 1: control register, written first without its gate to restart the note and then as given. 2: attack/decay. 3: sustain/release, whose low nybble also picks the release time from $8EC1. 4: pitch, an index into the frequency tables $9033/$9133. 5: pulse width high nybble (bits 0-3) and, with bit 7 set, the frequency halved bits 4-6 plus 1 times. 6: frames before the gate is released (128 and up: held until silenced). 7: offset of a 7-byte pitch envelope at $AC40, or 128 and up for none. Leaves the voice's state at $8E86-$8EBA for $8ED1 and $8F0C.
Low byte of the note's frequency while $8DB4 shifts it down octaves. The byte after it, $8E81, is not used.
Byte 5 of the sound block ($8DEC): pulse width high nybble in bits 0-3, bit 7 to lower the note, bits 4-6 how many more octaves.
The voice of the sound being started (byte 0), used to index the per-voice rows.
Counts the 7 envelope bytes copied into the voice's store ($8E59-$8E6D).
The A that $8F0C was called with (3, from $963A): an envelope steps only when its first byte ANDed with this is non-zero. 3 in the image.
Per voice (three bytes, the fourth unused as in all these rows): frames until the gate is released, from byte 6; 0 = done, 128 and up = held. Counted down by $8ED1.
Per voice: the current pitch index, from byte 4 and then moved by the envelope ($8F55).
Per voice: the release time in frames, looked up in $8EC1 by the low nybble of the sustain/release byte.
Per voice: frames left in the release; when it runs out $8ED1 silences the voice.
Per voice: where its envelope sits in $8EA6 (0, 7 or 14), or 128 and up when none is running. $FF in the image.
Per voice: steps left in the envelope's current section.
Per voice: the envelope section being stepped, 0-2.
Per voice: the control byte without its gate bit, written by $8ED1 when the note's time is up.

Three 7-byte pitch envelopes copied from $AC40 by $8DB4, for voices 0, 1, 2 at $8EA6, $8EAD, $8EB4. Byte 0 is read here: the envelope steps only if bits 0-1 are not both clear (with the mask in $8E85), and bit 7 set stops it after its third section instead of repeating.
Bytes 1-3 of an envelope: the pitch change per step in sections 1, 2 and 3, signed, read at $8F51.
Bytes 4-6 of an envelope: the number of steps in sections 1, 2 and 3 (0 skips the section), read at $8F41; the stores of voices 1 and 2 follow, to $8EBA.
SID register offset of each voice: 0, 7, 14 ($D400, $D407, $D40E).
Offset of each voice's envelope store in $8EA6: 0, 7, 14 (the same values, a separate table).
Frames to wait after the gate is released before the voice is silenced, by the release nybble 0-15: 1, 2, 3, 3, 6, 9, 11, 12, 15, 38, 75, 120, 150, 255, 255, 255.

Once a frame from the raster interrupt ($963D, through the JMP at $FFC2, the BBC's GSINIT slot). For each voice 2 to 0: counts the duration $8E86 down and at 0 releases the gate (control from $8EA2) and starts the release count from $8E8E; counts that down and at 0 turns the envelope off and silences the voice (sustain/release and control 0). Durations of 128 and up never count.

Once a frame from the raster interrupt ($963A, through the JMP at $FFC5, the BBC's GSREAD slot), A = 3. Steps each running pitch envelope whose first byte ANDs with A: counts the section's steps ($8E9A) and at the end of a section moves to the next of three ($8E9E, length from $8EAA); after the third it starts again unless bit 7 of the first byte ends it. Each step adds the section's change ($8EA7) to the pitch $8E8A and writes that pitch's frequency from $9033/$9133 to the voice. The pitch part of a BBC ENVELOPE, one step a frame.

OSBYTE, reached through the JMP at $FFF4. Two calls do something. A = $81 tests one key: jumps to $8CF9 with X = its C64 key number (the game's key numbers are C64 ones, e.g. the table at $138D). A = $15 silences voice X at once, X = 0-2 (the BBC flushes sound buffer X; the C64 callers at $351C pass voices): envelope and duration off, sustain/release and control cleared. Any other A returns doing nothing, $7E (acknowledge Escape, $8639) included.
The NMI handler ($FFFA, set by $8900): reads $DD0D to acknowledge CIA 2 and returns, A kept. Not entered in play (0 hits, live).

The interrupt handler $8900 installs ($FFFE): acknowledges both CIAs ($DC0D, $DD0D) and, if bit 7 of $D019 shows a VIC interrupt, the VIC ($D019 = $FF); only A is saved. $3F07 replaces it with the raster interrupt $95E9, and it is not entered in play (0 hits, live).

ASCII for each key number while a SHIFT key is down (OSRDCH, $8CEF = 0). Keys 0-7 are DEL ($7F), 3, 5, 7, 9, +, the pound key ($5C), 1; letters are capitals; RETURN $0D, SPACE $20, CLR/HOME $1E, up arrow $5E, both SHIFTs $10 (the scan skips them); function and cursor keys, CTRL, C=, RUN/STOP and the left arrow are 0.
ASCII for each key number with no SHIFT down ($8CEF = $40): as $8FB3 but letters in lower case, '?' for the / key (the shifted table has '/'), and 0 for the SHIFT keys. Runs to $9032.

SID frequency table, low bytes of entries 0-63 (high bytes at $9133). 256 entries indexed by a BBC-style pitch number: the C64's OSWORD 7 sound call ($8DF9, pitch from byte 4 of the parameter block) and the pitch-envelope update ($8F5C) fetch the 16-bit value for the voice's frequency registers. Entry n is round(2100 x 2^(n/48)) mod 65536, checked for all 256: 48 steps to the octave, i.e. quarter semitones, the step of the BBC Micro's SOUND pitch. Entry 0 is $0834, 123.3 Hz on a PAL machine; entry 48 is exactly double ($1068).
SID frequency table, low bytes of entries 64-127 (high bytes at $9173): from $14AC (entry 64, 310.8 Hz on PAL) to $3357 (entry 127, 771.8 Hz); entry 96 is $20D0, four times entry 0.
SID frequency table, low bytes of entries 128-191 (high bytes at $91B3): from $3416 (entry 128, 783.0 Hz on PAL) to $815E (entry 191, 1944.9 Hz); entry 144 is $41A0, eight times entry 0.

SID frequency table, low bytes of entries 192-255 (high bytes at $91F3). Entry 192 is $8340 (1973.2 Hz on PAL) and entry 238 $FF07 (3834 Hz); from entry 239 the formula needs 17 bits and the stored values have wrapped round ($02BD at 239 up to $45FD at 255), so pitches 239-255 would sound at 41-1052 Hz instead of carrying on upward.

SID frequency table, high bytes of entries 0-63 (low bytes at $9033): $08 up to $14. Before writing $D400/$D401 the OSWORD 7 handler can shift the pair right 1 to 8 places (bits 4-6 of parameter byte 5 plus one, when its bit 7 is set) to drop the note by octaves.
SID frequency table, high bytes of entries 64-127 (low bytes at $9073): $14 up to $33.
SID frequency table, high bytes of entries 128-191 (low bytes at $90B3): $34 up to $81.
SID frequency table, high bytes of entries 192-255 (low bytes at $90F3): $83 rising to $FF at entry 238, then $02 to $45 for the wrapped entries 239-255.
Not used: $9233-$927F hold a regular $FF $FF $00 $00 pattern with a stray $BF at $927C, like untouched RAM; no instruction found anywhere in the image refers to these addresses.

Zero-length exit of get_hypotenuse_angle ($9287), taken when both sides are 0 and A is 0: clears the side ratio $7E and the angle $8A/$8B, then returns. Byte for byte the BBC Micro code (BBC $5560, moved +$3D20).

Direction of a vector in the ground plane. In: |x| in $83 (high) / $80 (low) with x's sign in bit 7 of $86, |z| in $85 / $82 with z's sign in bit 7 of $88. Copies the longer side to $7B/$7A and the shorter to $5D/$5C (get_hypotenuse $937F uses them next), shifts both left until the longer fills 16 bits, divides through the arctangent routine at $0D4A (which also leaves the side ratio, 0-255, in $7E) and uses the two signs to put the result in the right quadrant. Out: angle in $8B (high byte, 256 to a full turn) and $8A. Called from $288C, $3749, $37C4, $8410, $84DD and $935B. The BBC routine (BBC $5567) with only its own addresses moved.

Pitch of a vector as seen from object X, relative to where that object is looking. In: the vertical component in A (high) and $80 (low), the ground distance in $7D/$7C, X the viewing object. Keeps the sign in $86, makes the vertical side absolute ($83/$80), calls get_hypotenuse_angle with the distance as the other side (sign 0 in $88), subtracts the object's pitch ($0140,X, with $20 as low byte) and divides by 16 with the sign kept: result in $8D (high) and $50. Called from $18E6, $20BB, $292D, $8516. The BBC routine (BBC $561D), relocated.

Length of the hypotenuse without a square root: the longer side ($7B/$7A) plus the shorter side ($5D/$5C) times tan(half the angle), the tangent from the table at $3D02 indexed by half the ratio in $7E (rounded) and multiplied in by $0F4A. Result in $7D/$7C. Y is kept in hyp_saved_y ($93AD) and given back. Called from $28A0, $3779, $8438, $84F3. The BBC routine (BBC $565F), relocated.
Where get_hypotenuse keeps the caller's Y (stored at $937F, reloaded at $93A9). $3F in the hand-over image; the BBC binary has $41 at this spot, a leftover value either way.

Step the 24-bit random generator at $93EF-$93F1 and return its top byte in A: copies it to $93F2-$93F4, shifts the copy left two places and adds it back, so the generator is multiplied by 5 modulo 2^24 (it starts at 1). The same code as the BBC's (BBC $568E), but in the C64 program only the two dot routines call it: draw_stars ($9403) and the black-dot fade ($9464).
Random generator, lowest byte of the 24-bit value next_random multiplies by 5 on each call; 01 00 00 in the image, so the sequence is 5, 25, 125, ... modulo 2^24.

Random generator, middle byte; the dot routines also use it as a second random number: draw_stars takes its low five bits for the dot's page and its top two bits for the pixel ($9408), the black-dot fade its low six bits for the column step ($9480).
Random generator, top byte: the value next_random returns in A. The black-dot fade also takes its top two bits as the pixel within the byte ($94A9).
Scratch for next_random: the generator's low byte, copied and shifted left twice before being added back.
Scratch for next_random: middle byte of the generator times four.
Scratch for next_random: top byte of the generator times four (bits shifted out of it are lost, hence modulo 2^24).

Draw 40 random stars in colour 2 (%10) into the view picture at $E000, the bitmap that show_whole_view ($98B2) copies to the screen. Called three times by the screen-clearing routine at $1090 when the background type $0C4C is 3, so 120 stars. For each dot: a random low byte (next_random) and a random page 0-$1D (low five bits of $93F0, retried if above) added to the view address $0CC2/$0CC3; a random pixel 0-3 from the top bits of $93F0; the pixel is cleared with the mask at $228E, set to colour 1 from $945B and flipped to colour 2 because bit 7 of dot_colour is set. Differs from the BBC routine (BBC $56D5): 40 dots instead of 80, multicolour pixel tables, the wrap test turned round for a picture that ends at $FFFF (take $20 off the page when the add carries past $FF, where the BBC did so at $80), and a check ($9427) that skips a dot at $FF40 or above, where the vectors and entry-point jumps live. The screen-clearing routine sets $0CC2/$0CC3 to $E140 ($1336) just before, so the highest address reached is $FF3F and neither the wrap nor the skip happens there.
LDA #0 here is the BBC's DrawBlackDots entry (colour 1 dots); nothing in the C64 program calls $93F9
40 dots per call; the BBC drew 80
C64: a page add that carried past $FF comes back as $00-$1F, so take $20 off
C64 guard: no dot at $FF40-$FFFF (vectors and entry-point jumps)
Dots left to draw: 40 from draw_stars ($9400) or the caller's count in the black-dot fade ($9461); counted down at $9453 and $94C9.

Bit 7 set: draw_stars flips each dot from colour 1 to colour 2 (set to $80 at $93FB through the draw_stars entry; the unused entry at $93F9 would store 0 for colour 1). $00 in the hand-over image, $80 in play.

Colour 1 (%01) in each of the four multicolour pixels of a byte, indexed by pixel 0-3: $40, $10, $04, $01; ORed in by draw_stars ($9446) and the black-dot fade ($94B9). The BBC's table here held its own pixel layout (08 04 02 01).

Game-over fade: draw 27 random black (colour 1) dots straight into the play view's character sets, then return; the C64's stand-in for the BBC's DrawBlackDots. Used by the screen decay loop at $8801, which calls it 30 times per pass ($8807). Falls into fade_view_dots with A = 27.

Draw A random colour-1 (black) dots into the play view's character sets. The raster interrupt calls it with A = 4 on four of its five band interrupts whenever bit 7 of $0C4D is set ($962A), and with A = 12 on the fifth when the Sentinel has also won ($9697). Row: the random walk dot_row_walk (0-23) plus the vertical scroll position $95, wrapped at 25, looked up in the row tables at $3A00 (low) / $3A20 (high); $3A40 gives the page offset of a second character set for rows that straddle two bands. Byte: the random walk dot_byte_walk (0-79) within the row. Pixel: the top two bits of $93F1. Each dot is written four times, 80 bytes (10 cells) apart across the row, and into both character sets of a split row. Not in the BBC program, which drew its dots into screen memory.
each dot at Y = $F0, $A0, $50, $00: four places 80 bytes apart
Row of the last fade dot, 0-23: each dot adds a random 0-15 and wraps at 24 ($9464-$9473); the vertical scroll $95 is added on top.
Byte offset of the last fade dot within its character row, 0-79 (cells 0-9, pixel row = offset mod 8): each dot adds a random 0-63 and wraps at 80 ($9480-$9491).
Not used: $94D1-$94FF hold a regular $FF $FF $00 $00 pattern with a stray $BF at $94FC, like untouched RAM; no instruction found anywhere in the image refers to these addresses.

Multicolour pixel masks, eight entries: 0-3 ($3F, $CF, $F3, $FC) clear one pixel of a byte, pixels 0-3 from the left; 4-7 ($C0, $30, $0C, $03) keep only that pixel. The black-dot fade uses entries 0-3 ($94B6); the dithering code at $8783 indexes all eight (X = $0CD0 / 32, then X EOR 3). The C64 counterpart of the BBC's clearPixelMask (BBC $36BF, 77 BB DD EE 88 44 22 11).

Rewrite the top screen row, the energy icons and the scanner frame: the player's energy ($0C0A) drawn as gold robots (icon 6, 15 units each, each followed by a blank), robots (icon 1, 3 units), then a boulder (icons 4-5, 2 units) or a tree (icons 2-3, 1 unit) for what is left; blanks up to column 29; the scanner box (icon 7, icon 8 up to column 38, icon 9) and a final blank. The column counter is $0C05, the working total $15. The same arithmetic as the BBC's UpdateIconsScanner (BBC $36C7), but each icon is one character written into the screen matrix by put_icon_char, and it ends with RTS where the BBC went on to copy an icon buffer to the screen. Called from $12FF, $1A1A, $35C6. In the play snapshot the row reads robot, robot, robot, tree: 10 units.

Put icon A (0-9) at the next column of the top row: stores character $F0 + A in the screen matrix at $7C00 + $0C05 and advances $0C05; A is preserved. The icon glyphs are characters $F0-$F9, copied into all five character sets from $ABB0 by show_whole_view ($98E8). Replaces the BBC's DrawIcon, which copied eight pixel bytes per icon.
Which of the five screen bands (0-4) the raster interrupt set up last: counted down by one at each interrupt, 0 wrapping to 4 ($95FF-$9607); set by set_band_lines ($95C9). $03 in the play snapshot.

Raster line of each band's interrupt, bands 0-4, worked out from the vertical scroll position $95 by set_band_lines: 53, 213, 173, 133, 93 when $95 is 0 (as in the image). The interrupt that starts band X shows its character set until the line in entry X.

$D018 value for each band 0-4: $F8, $F6, $F4, $F2, $F0, the screen matrix at $7C00 with the character set at $6000, $5800, $5000, $4800 and $4000 (VIC bank 1); written at $95DA and $9618. With $95 = 0 this gives $4000 from line 53, $4800 from 93, $5000 from 133, $5800 from 173 and $6000 from 213 to the next frame's line 53, the writes seen live at lines 54-214.

Index of the band whose interrupt also does the once-a-frame work at $9630 (sound, keys, enemy timers): the band whose line is below 91, set at $95C0; 0 in the image, which puts the work at line 213. The next byte, $9594, is not referenced.

Work out the band interrupt lines for the vertical scroll position $95 (0-24): band 0 at $FD - 8 x $95, bands 4, 3, 2, 1 each 40 lines further on, every value brought into lines 51-250 by adding or taking 200, stored in band_lines. The band whose line is below 91 becomes frame_band. Then starts the sequence at that band: band_index, raster compare $D012 (bit 8 in $D011 cleared) and its character set in $D018. C64 only; called from show_whole_view ($98BC).
Exit for an interrupt that did not come from the VIC (bit 7 of $D019 clear, $95EE): reads $DC0D and $DD0D to clear any CIA interrupt, restores A and returns from the interrupt.

The game's interrupt handler (the IRQ vector at $FFFE is set to $95E9 at $3F08); the C64 replacement for the BBC's IRQHandler. Acknowledges the raster interrupt, saves X and Y. If video_mode_flag ($9AF6) is set (play view) it steps band_index down, arms the next band's raster line and switches $D018 to that band's character set; on the four bands other than frame_band it then only draws fade dots when bit 7 of $0C4D is set (fade_view_dots, A = 4) and returns. On frame_band's interrupt, or on every interrupt when $9AF6 is 0 (one a frame, no bands), it does the once-a-frame work: counts down the sound timer $0CDF, calls $FFC5 with A = 3 and $FFC2 (the C64 sound update at $8F0C and $8ED1, behind the BBC GSREAD and GSINIT addresses), and while a game is in progress ($0CFC bit 7 clear): on a Sentinel win ($0C4E) draws fade dots (A = 12) if $0C4D bit 7 is set; when paused ($0C72) scans the keys with $1363 (Y = 13, the BBC's ScanForGameKeys) and clears key-logger entries 0-2 ($0CE8-$0CEA); otherwise sets bit 7 of $0CD8 while pan steps are pending ($0CC1 non-zero), calls $130C and $1635 (the BBC's enemy-timer and scanner updates) when the Sentinel is active ($0CE5 bit 7 clear) and no step is flagged, and calls the key check $119F unless $0CE4 bit 7 is set or the countdown at $130B is still running. The BBC handler ran the pan scroll itself; here the pan loop at $3668 waits for the $0CD8 flag instead.
0 = bitmap screen: no bands, straight to the frame work
C64 sound update through the BBC GSREAD/GSINIT addresses
C64: flag one pan step for the loop at $3668 instead of scrolling here
C64: key scan held off while $130B counts down (set to 2 at $1286)

How far the sights sprite moves for one pan step, by direction 0-3 (right, left, up, down): -8 and +8 pixels in X ($D000) for right and left, +8 and -8 lines in Y ($D001) for up and down, against the scroll, so the sights stay on the same spot of the landscape (scroll_view_step, $96DA and $971F).
High-byte partner for the sights' X move: $FF for a pan right, $00 for a pan left, added with the carry into $D010 ($96E3), whose bit 0 is sprite 0's X bit 8.

One step of a pan, the C64's counterpart of the BBC's ScrollPlayerView; called from the pan loop at $366D each time the interrupt has flagged $0CD8. Y = the pan direction from $08 (0 right, 1 left, 2 up, 3 down). Right or left: moves the column position $94 by +1 or -1 (0-39, wrapping), sets $96 to the column to fill ($94 + 39 for right, $94 for left, mod 40) and $97 to the row position $95. Up or down: moves the row position $95 by -1 or +1 (0-24, wrapping), sets $97 to the row to fill ($95 for up, $95 + 23 for down, mod 25) and $96 to $94. While the sights are shown ($0C5F bit 7) it moves sprite 0 eight pixels against the scroll (sights_pan_step) and copies the sights position $0CC6 or $0CC7 to $9B or $9C. Ends by counting down the steps left in $0CC1. It changes no screen address and moves no picture data: the pan loop calls $B006 next, which is missing from this copy.
move the sights sprite with the landscape

Two bytes of code that nothing calls (no reference found by address anywhere in the image): LDY $08, the pan direction, falling into show_buffer_strip. The BBC's ScrollPlayerView began with the same instruction; the C64's only caller of $9730 ($207C) loads Y itself.

Copy the strip of picture a pan step reveals from the view picture at $E000 into the character sets, the C64 rewrite of the BBC's ShowScreenBuffer. Y = direction 0-3. First advances the source pointer $2095/$2096 by one cell column (+8 or -8) or one character row (-$140 or +$140) from pan_source_step, then: up or down, copies a whole 40-cell row through copy_buffer_row ($979D); right or left, copies one column of 24 cells, into column $96 of the character-set rows from $97 down (wrapping after row 24): cell address = row base from $3A00/$3A20 plus 8 x $96, copied again through the $3A40 page offset for rows that straddle two character sets, the source moving down $140 a row since the picture is laid out as a C64 bitmap. Called from $207E.

Copy one character row of the picture (40 cells, 320 bytes from $62/$63) into row $97 of the character-set buffer, starting at column $96 and wrapping round: 40 - $96 cells to the right-hand end, then the pointer taken back $140 for the remaining $96 cells at columns 0 onward. Rows that straddle two character sets ($3A40,X non-zero) are written twice through copy_cells_twice with the second address in $99/$9A (page offset kept in split_row_page); the others through copy_cells. Used by show_buffer_strip for up and down pans and by show_whole_view for every row.

Page offset from a split row's first character set to its second ($08 for rows crossing a band boundary, $20 for the row wrapping from $6000 to $4000), kept by copy_buffer_row ($97DF) to rebuild the second pointer $9A after the wrap ($9808). $00 in the image, $20 in play.

Copy X cells of 8 bytes from ($62),Y to both ($64),Y and ($99),Y, Y carrying on from its entry value and the three pointers' high bytes stepped each time Y wraps: the double write for character rows that show in two bands.
Copy X cells of 8 bytes from ($62),Y to ($64),Y, Y carrying on from its entry value and both pointers' high bytes stepped each time Y wraps.
Copy one 8-byte cell from ($62) to ($64), Y = 0 to 7. The BBC's ShowBufferBlock byte for byte (BBC $38B2); used by show_buffer_strip for column pans.

Put the whole view picture on the play screen; called from $35C9, after $2625 (the BBC's DrawLandscapeView) has drawn the landscape into the picture. Resets the scroll positions $94-$97 to 0 and recomputes the band lines (set_band_lines); sets $D027 and $D025 to 6 (blue), centres the sights ($134C) and places sprite 0 there (place_sights_sprite); copies all 25 character rows of the picture into the character-set buffer with copy_buffer_row, the source rows taken from $3D9C/$3DCE ($E140, $E280, ... $FE00, then $E000); copies the ten icon characters from $ABB0 into characters $F0-$F9 of all five character sets ($4780, $4F80, $5780, $5F80, $6780); turns sprite 0 off again (hide_sights_sprite) and sets $D027 to 1 (white) and $D025 to 0 (black), the sights' colours.

Offset from the new scroll position to the column or row a pan step must fill, by direction 0-3: +39 (right: the right-hand column), 0 (left), 0 (up: the top row), +23 (down: the bottom row); read by scroll_view_step at $96C1 and $9707.
Change to the scroll position for one pan step, by direction 0-3: +1 (right, column position $94), -1 (left), -1 (up, row position $95), +1 (down); read at $96AF and $96F5.

Low bytes of the step added to the pan source pointer $2095/$2096 before each copy, by direction 0-3: +8, -8, -$140, +$140, one cell column or one character row of the view picture (high bytes at $9919). The same values as the BBC's scrollScreenLo/Hi.
High bytes of the pan source step, by direction 0-3: $00, $FF, $FE, $01 (low bytes at $9915).

High bytes of the pan source pointer's starting value, by direction 0-3, giving $E138, $E1C0, $EB40 and $E000 with the low bytes at $9921: one step before the first cell or row to copy, since show_buffer_strip adds the step first; all inside the view picture at $E000. The BBC's screenBufferHi/Lo pointed into a separate buffer instead.
Low bytes of the pan source starting values, by direction 0-3: $38, $C0, $40, $00 (high bytes at $991D).

Angle change used while the new strip of a pan is drawn, by direction 0-3: +20, -8 (added to the player's yaw $09C0,X at $10C3 and taken off at $10F8), +4, -12 (added to the pitch $0140,X at $1108 and taken off at $1142). The same values as the BBC's panAngleToUpdate.

Start a pan: store the number of pan steps, A, in $0CD1 (the pan loop at $3660 copies it to the step counter $0CC1), then fall into set_pan_source for direction Y. Called from $10F0 and $1137. The BBC's StartScrollingView.

Set the pan source pointer $2095/$2096 to the starting address for direction Y from pan_source_start ($9921 low, $991D high). Also called on its own from $202E with Y = 0. The BBC's SetBufferAddress with C64 addresses in the table.

Get ready to draw the new rows of an up or down pan: calls $2993 with A = 0 (the buffer set-up, the BBC's ConfigureBuffer), then sets the pitch limits $51 = $F0 and $52 = $B0 (entry 0 of buffer_max_pitch and buffer_min_pitch). Called from $111C. The BBC's UseRowBuffer with its call relocated.
Upper pitch limit written to $51 while drawing a pan strip: $F0 for rows (entry 0) and for columns (entry 1). The BBC's values.
Lower pitch limit written to $52 while drawing a pan strip: $B0 for rows (entry 0), $30 for columns (entry 1). The BBC's values.
Get ready to draw the new columns of a left or right pan: calls $2993 with A = 2, then falls into set_column_buffer_pitch. Called from $10D7. The BBC's UseColumnBuffer.
Set the pitch limits for column strips, $51 = $F0 and $52 = $30 (entry 1 of $994B/$994D), by jumping into use_row_buffer's tail with Y = 1. Called from $113A and $1196.

Move the sights one step for the keys in the key logger: sideways (move_sights_sideways), then, if bit 7 of $09 is still set (no sideways pan started), up or down (move_sights_up_down), then show sprite 0 at the new place (place_sights_sprite). Called from $11FB. The BBC's MoveSights ended by drawing the sights into screen memory instead.

Move the sights' x position $0CC6 by one for key-logger entry 0 ($0CE8: 0 right, 1 left, bit 7 no key), within $10-$8F: a step past either edge takes it $40 back towards the middle and stores the direction in $09, which starts a pan. The new x, before any wrap, is copied to $9B for the sprite. The BBC routine's logic without its screen-address update.

Move the sights' y position $0CC7 by one for key-logger entry 2 ($0CEA: 2 up, 3 down, bit 7 no key), within $20-$9F: a step past the top or bottom takes it $40 back and stores the direction in $09 (a pan up or down), unless the player's pitch ($0140 + object $0B) is already at its limit ($35 at $114B going up, $CD at $114C going down), when y stays where it was. The new y goes to $9C for the sprite, put back to the old value at a limit ($99D6). The BBC routine plus the $9C bookkeeping.

Show the sights as sprite 0 at the sights position: Y register $D001 = $F9 - $9C, X = 2 x $9B + 14 with bit 8 put into bit 0 of $D010 (through sights_x_high), then sprite 0 enabled in $D015. Does nothing while bit 7 of $0CD7 is set. Sprite 0's image (pointer $C0, data at $7000, drawn by $3F13-$3F5F) is a cross 11 multicolour pixels wide and 11 lines high whose pixels alternate between the sprite colour and multicolour 0 (white and black once show_whole_view has set them). The C64's replacement for the BBC's DrawSights, which drew the cross into screen memory. Called from $11C7, $208E, $98CA, $9962.
sprite Y = $F9 - sights y
sprite X = 2 x sights x + 14, nine bits
Scratch: bit 8 of the sights sprite's X position while place_sights_sprite builds it ($99EB-$9A07).

Not read by any code found (searched for its addresses throughout the image): three 4-byte multicolour tables, pixel-clear masks $3F $CF $F3 $FC, colour 1 $40 $10 $04 $01 and colour 2 $80 $20 $08 $02. They look like the C64 conversion of the pixel tables the BBC's DrawSights used, left behind when the sights became a sprite.

Not read by any code found: 12 bytes identical to the BBC's xSightsStep (00 00 00 FB 02 02 02 02 02 FB 00 00), the horizontal half of the pixel path along which the BBC drew its cross; unused here, where the sights are sprite 0.
Not read by any code found: 13 bytes identical to the BBC's ySightsStep (00 02 02 01 00 00 00 00 00 01 02 02 and the end marker $80), the vertical half of that pixel path.
Hide the sights: clear bit 0 of $D015, sprite 0 off. Replaces the BBC's RemoveSights, which put back the screen bytes under its drawn cross. Called from $11CD, $1FAF, $205F, $98FF.
Not read by any code found: 6 bytes identical to the BBC's sightsMoveAddrLo (08 F8 FF 01 C7 39), screen-address steps for moving its drawn cross; high bytes at $9A4B.
Not read by any code found: 6 bytes identical to the BBC's sightsMoveAddrHi (00 FF FF 00 FE 01), the partner of $9A45.

Switch the display between the bitmap screens (title, landscape overview) and the play view; A is stored in video_mode_flag. Bit 7 clear (from $117E with A = 0): VIC bank 3 ($DD00 bits 0-1 = 00), multicolour bitmap at $E000 with its screen colours at $CC00 ($D011 = $3B, $D018 = $38), colour RAM filled with the low three bits of $D800's colour, raster interrupt at line 100. Bit 7 set (from $3577 with A = $80, as a game starts): VIC bank 1 (bits = 10), multicolour text, matrix $7C00, characters from $4000 ($D011 = $1B, $D018 = $F0), colour RAM filled with $D800's colour OR 8 (each cell's multicolour flag), sprite multicolour 1 ($D026) = 5, then falls into reset_view_matrix.

Fill the play screen matrix: rows 0-23 ($7C00-$7FBF) with character codes 0-239 in four runs of 240, so the pattern repeats every six rows; row 24 ($7FC0-$7FE7) with $28-$4F; and $7FE8 with 0. With the band interrupts giving each 40 lines its own character set, every cell of the view has its own 8 bytes, a bitmap built from characters. Row 0 is then overwritten by update_icon_row. Also called from $1347, after $94 and $95 are set to 0.
Fill all of colour RAM, $D800-$DBFF, with A. Called by set_video_mode and from $8674.

Display mode: bit 7 set = the play view (character sets with band interrupts), clear = a bitmap screen. Written only by set_video_mode; read by play_irq ($95FA, zero = one interrupt a frame and no band switching), $283D and $866D (whether colour RAM gets the multicolour bit). $00 in the hand-over image, $80 in play.

Not used: $9AF7-$9C02 hold a regular $FF $FF $00 $00 pattern, its phase changing at $9B00, with stray values at $9AFC and $9B7E ($BF) and $9BFC ($40), like untouched RAM; no instruction found anywhere in the image refers to these addresses.

Not used by the game: $9C03-$9C9F is a piece of the BBC BASIC interpreter. BRK, error number 19 and 'String too long' with its closing zero ($9C03-$9C14), then the code that raises it: string concatenation through BASIC's string buffer at $0600 (BCS $9C03 at $9C27 when the combined length passes 255) and 32-bit integer addition on $2A-$2D, with calls to $8C0E-$BDCB. Its absolute jumps land on instruction boundaries of the other fragments (JSR $9DD1 at $9C42 and $9C8E, JSR $9DCE at $9C53), which fits the pieces sitting at the addresses the interpreter runs from. Nothing in the game refers to them.

First point number of each object type, 11 bytes, read at $8480 with X = the type ($4C): 0, 29, 51, 68, 76, 94, 124, 136, 144, 152, then 160 to close the list. In the BBC program the types are robot, sentry, tree, boulder, meanie, the Sentinel, its tower and three blocks of the large 3D title text. Identical to the BBC table (BBC $49A0, moved +$5300).
The point table read one entry on ($847B): the first point of the next type, where type X's points stop: 29, 51, 68, 76, 94, 124, 136, 144, 152, 160.

First polygon number of each object type, read at $8576: 0, 27, 52, 67, 77, 102, 137, 148, 152, 156, then 160. For polygon n the drawing code reads a data byte at $A1A0 + n ($857B) and finds the point list through the address tables $A2E0/$A420 + n. Identical to the BBC table.
The polygon table read one entry on ($8571): where type X's polygons stop: 27, 52, 67, 77, 102, 137, 148, 152, 156, 160.

How each object type is drawn, read at $854D: 0 = one pass (types 2, 3, 6-9); 3 = two passes chosen by the object's height relative to the viewer ($0C5C/$0C5B; types 0, 1, 5); 2 = two passes chosen by the object's yaw ($5A; type 4). The eleventh byte ($9CC0) is 0 and unused. Identical to the BBC table.

Not read or written by any code found: 12 bytes where the BBC version kept the low bytes of the screen addresses under its drawn sights (BBC $49C1). The first five are $00 as in the BBC binary; the last seven, $04 $E5 $2A $85 $2A $C8 $B1, differ and read as more BASIC interpreter code (SBC $2A, STA $2A, INY, LDA (..),Y).

Point lists of the meanie's polygons 77-89, found through the polygon address tables at $A2E0 (low) and $A420 (high) rather than by direct reference. Each byte is $40 plus a point number counted from the meanie's first point, 76, and each list ends by repeating its first point: polygon 77 is $47 $4C $4B $46 $47, points 83, 88, 87, 82 and back to 83. Identical to the BBC data (BBC $49CD).

Point lists of the meanie's polygons 90-101, in the same form as at $9CCD: polygon 90 is $47 $4D $4C $47; polygon 101, $4F $51 $50 $4E $4F, ends the block at $9D36. The highest byte used, $51, is point 93, the meanie's last.

How far each enemy turns at a time, one byte per enemy (X): set at $1586 to $14 (+20) or $EC (-20), picked by the low bit of the number from $31CA, and added to the enemy's yaw $09C0,X at $180D; 20 of the 256 units in a turn is 28.1 degrees. Nine bytes as in the BBC ($9D37-$9D3F). Until a landscape is set up they hold BBC BASIC bytes (see $9D40); in the play snapshot $9D37 = $EC.
