Not used by the game: $9D40-$9DDF is more BBC BASIC interpreter code at its own address: 32-bit shift-and-add multiplication on $2A-$2D and $39-$40, and the start of the expression level for '*', '/' and MOD ($9DD4: CPX #$2A, reached by JMP $9DD4 at $9DC8). The BBC version kept a row of its screen buffer here (BBC $4A40).

Angle of each object point around its object's vertical axis, 256 to the turn: points 0-50 (robot 0-28, sentry 29-50 in BBC terms). Added to the object's own yaw ($5A) at $848C; the point's distance from the axis is at $A060 + n and its height at $9F20 + n. Identical to the BBC table (BBC $4AE0).
Object point angles continued: points 51-93 (tree 51-67, boulder 68-75, meanie 76-93).
Object point angles continued: points 94-135 (the Sentinel 94-123, its tower 124-135).
Object point angles continued: points 136-159, the three 3D text blocks (136-143, 144-151, 152-159); the table ends at $9E7F.

Not used by the game: $9E80-$9F1F is more BBC BASIC interpreter code, apparently number output: hexadecimal digits and a minus sign sent through $A066, and a loop (JMP $9ED1 at $9EDC) that lands on the LDA $30 at $9ED1, an instruction boundary. The BBC version kept another screen-buffer row here (BBC $4B80).

Height of each object point relative to the object's origin: points 0-50. Bits 0-6 are half the size and bit 7 the sign: $84F8 doubles the byte and negates the result through $1009 when bit 7 was set ($F0 gives -224), then adds the object's height relative to the viewer ($0C5B/$0C5C). Identical to the BBC table (BBC $4C20).
Object point heights continued: points 51-93 (tree, boulder, meanie).
Object point heights continued: points 94-135 (the Sentinel and its tower).
Object point heights continued: points 136-159 (the 3D text blocks); the table ends at $9FBF.

Not used by the game: from $9FC0 on past $A000 is BBC BASIC interpreter code at its own address, more of its number printing ('0' and '.' sent through $A066). The BBC version kept another screen-buffer row here (BBC $4CC0).

Not the game's: 96 bytes of BBC BASIC's own code, at the address the BASIC ROM occupies on a BBC Micro, left in a gap between the game's tables. They are the tail of BASIC's number-to-text routine: it strips trailing zeros and a trailing point from the digits in BASIC's string buffer ($0600, length in $36), then appends 'E', a minus sign and the exponent's digits (split off by the divide-by-ten loop at $A052). No instruction in the game refers to $A000-$A05F and the bytes are the same at the hand-over and in play. The BBC original keeps a screen-buffer row at the matching place (this address minus $5300).

Object shapes: the distance of each shape point from its object's vertical axis, one byte per point for points 0-159 of the ten object types (each type's first point is in the table at $9CA0; the point's yaw is at $9DE0 and its height at $9F20, same index). $8494 and $84C9 multiply the distance by the sine and cosine ($0F70, $0D03) of the point's yaw plus the object's, giving the point's offsets across the ground. Type names follow the BBC reconstruction; the C64's energy table at $214F agrees for the robot (3 units), tree (1) and boulder (2). This label: the robot, object type 0, points 0-28, distances 0 to 56. The whole table is byte for byte the BBC original's.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the sentry, object type 1: points 29-50, 22 bytes, distances 31 to 64.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the tree, object type 2: points 51-67, 17 bytes, distances 0 to 104.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the boulder, object type 3: points 68-75, all eight at distance 112.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the meanie, object type 4: points 76-93, 18 bytes, distances 12 to 68.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the Sentinel, object type 5: points 94-123, 30 bytes, distances 19 to 70.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the Sentinel's tower, object type 6: points 124-135, 12 bytes, distances 145 to 181.
Point distances (format at $A060) for the three 3D text blocks, object types 7, 8 and 9: points 136-143, 144-151 and 152-159, eight each, distances 136 to 192.

Not the game's: 160 bytes of BBC BASIC at its ROM address, between the point distances and the polygon data. They belong to BASIC's reader for decimal numbers: a loop that scales by ten once per step of the decimal exponent in $49 ($A102-$A11E), a reader for an exponent's sign and one or two digits taken from the program text through ($19),Y ($A140-$A177), and a five-byte mantissa add ($A178). Nothing in the game refers to $A100-$A19F; the BBC original has screen-buffer row 12 at the matching place.

Object shapes: one byte per polygon for polygons 0-159 of the ten object types (each type's first polygon is in the table at $9CAB). Bits 0-1: number of sides less three ($858E; only triangles and quadrilaterals occur). Bits 2-3: fill colour, bits 4-5: edge colour ($8587 passes both to the polygon drawer in $19; $22E2 swaps the edge colour for the fill colour when the object's distance byte $7D is $0F or more, the flag set at $8536). Bit 6: always clear. Bit 7: which of the two passes draws the polygon, for the types that are drawn in two ($8582, the type's setting at $9CB6). This label: the robot, polygons 0-26, 12 triangles and 15 quadrilaterals, 16 in the second pass. Byte for byte the BBC original's table.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the sentry, object type 1: polygons 27-51, 12 triangles and 13 quadrilaterals, 16 of them in the second pass.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the tree, object type 2: polygons 52-66, 8 triangles and 7 quadrilaterals, all drawn in one pass.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the boulder, object type 3: polygons 67-76, 8 triangles and 2 quadrilaterals, one pass.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the meanie, object type 4: polygons 77-101, 19 triangles and 6 quadrilaterals, 3 of them in the second pass.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the Sentinel, object type 5: polygons 102-136, 16 triangles and 19 quadrilaterals, 21 of them in the second pass.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the Sentinel's tower, object type 6: polygons 137-147, 4 triangles and 7 quadrilaterals, one pass.
Polygon data (bits as at $A1A0) for the three 3D text blocks, object types 7-9: polygons 148-159, four quadrilaterals per block.

Not the game's: 160 bytes of BBC BASIC at its ROM address, between the polygon data and the low bytes of the polygon list addresses. Most of it is a floating-point divide by ten ($A24D: it takes 4 from the exponent in $30, then scales the mantissa with a chain of shifts and adds), after the tail of a mantissa shift ($A242: LSR $3E, then ROR $3F to $42). Nothing in the game refers to $A240-$A2DF; the BBC original has screen-buffer row 13 at the matching place.

Object shapes: low bytes of the address of each polygon's point list, polygons 0-159. The high bytes are 320 bytes on, at $A420; the BASIC leftover at $A380 lies between the halves. $8595 and $859A load the pair into $3C/$3D for the polygon drawer at $2AA9. The lists are at $A560-$A79F for every type but the meanie, whose lists are at $9CCD-$9D36. This label: the robot, polygons 0-26, lists at $A6B4-$A72E. Same bytes as the BBC original's, since the lists moved by a whole number of pages.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the sentry: polygons 27-51, lists at $A72F-$A79F.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the tree: polygons 52-66, lists at $A600-$A642.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the boulder: polygons 67-76, lists at $A643-$A66C.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the meanie: polygons 77-101, lists at $9CCD-$9D36.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the Sentinel: polygons 102-136, lists at $A560-$A5FE.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the Sentinel's tower: polygons 137-147, lists at $A66D-$A69F.
Polygon list addresses, low bytes (see $A2E0), for the three 3D text blocks: polygons 148-159, each block's four pointing at the same four lists at $A6A0-$A6B3.

Not the game's: 160 bytes of BBC BASIC at its ROM address, between the two halves of the polygon list address table. They include BASIC's store of its floating-point accumulator as a five-byte number at $046C or $0476 ($A381) and the reverse, loading one through the pointer in $4B/$4C into the accumulator ($A3B5). Nothing in the game refers to $A380-$A41F; the BBC original has screen-buffer row 14 at the matching place.

Object shapes: high bytes of the polygon point-list addresses, polygons 0-159 (low bytes at $A2E0). Each is the BBC original's value plus $53, the lists having moved up by $5300: $A5, $A6 or $A7 for the lists at $A560-$A79F, $9C or $9D for the meanie's. This label: the robot, polygons 0-26, $A6 and $A7.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the sentry: polygons 27-51, all $A7.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the tree: polygons 52-66, all $A6.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the boulder: polygons 67-76, all $A6.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the meanie: polygons 77-101, $9C and $9D.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the Sentinel: polygons 102-136, all $A5.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the Sentinel's tower: polygons 137-147, all $A6.
Polygon list addresses, high bytes (see $A420), for the three 3D text blocks: polygons 148-159, all $A6.

Not the game's: 160 bytes of BBC BASIC at its ROM address, between the polygon list addresses and the Sentinel's polygon lists: part of BASIC's floating-point arithmetic, with short entries that chain its routines ($A4C7, $A4D0), a copy of the second operand ($3B-$42) into the accumulator ($2E-$35) at $A4D6, and the start of another routine at $A4FD. Nothing in the game refers to $A4C0-$A55F; the BBC original has screen-buffer row 15 at the matching place.

Object shapes, polygon point lists: each polygon lists its corners in order and repeats the first to close it (sides + 1 bytes). An entry is 64 + the point's number within its object, because the object's points are projected into the drawing tables from entry 64 on ($8477, $84E0), and the polygon drawer uses the entry directly as that index ($2D99). Lists for the Sentinel, object type 5 (points 94-123), run from here to $A5FE; this label: polygons 102-115.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the Sentinel: polygons 116-129.

Point lists (format at $A560) for the Sentinel: polygons 130-136, ending at $A5FE. The byte at $A5FF after them is a spare that no polygon address points at ($3E here, $10 at the BBC original's matching place).
Point lists (format at $A560) for the tree, object type 2 (points 51-67): polygons 52-58.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the tree: polygons 59-66, ending at $A642.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the boulder, object type 3 (points 68-75): polygons 67-76.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the Sentinel's tower, object type 6 (points 124-135): polygons 137-147.

Point lists (format at $A560) shared by the three 3D text blocks, object types 7-9: four quadrilaterals over entries 64-71 (a block's eight points), used alike for polygons 148-151, 152-155 and 156-159, since each entry counts from its own object's first point.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the robot, object type 0 (points 0-28): polygons 0-12.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the robot: polygons 13-26, ending at $A72E.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the sentry, object type 1 (points 29-50): polygons 27-39.
Point lists (format at $A560) for the sentry: polygons 40-51, ending at $A79F.

Run-time buffer, 96 bytes to $A7FF, one byte per drawing-table entry: the low byte of the screen x-coordinate of each corner of the polygon being drawn, worked out at $2D99-$2DEC as the corner's yaw ($0BA0 low, $A800 high, plus the offset in $29/$11) divided by 32, the high byte going to $0B40. The edge tracer reads it ($2E79, $2ECC, $3008, $3049, $30A6). Entries 0-63 are tile corners (two rows of 32), 64-95 the points of the object being drawn. What the image holds here is stale: BBC BASIC's SQR routine ($A7B4, whose BMI at $A7BC reaches the error block at $A7A9: BRK, error 21, '-ve root') and noise. Play overwrites it.

Entries 64-95 of the screen x low bytes (see $A7A0): the points of the object being drawn. Stale in the image; $A7E8-$A7FD hold the same 22 bytes as the BBC original's workspace at the matching place.

Run-time buffer, 96 bytes to $A85F: the high byte of the yaw angle, measured from the left edge of the view, of each drawing-table entry (low bytes at $0BA0, pitch at $0A80 and $0AE0). Entries 0-31 and 32-63 hold the corners of two neighbouring rows of tiles, the drawing code swapping halves after each row (it flips the offset in $05 by 32 at $26E0); entries 64-95 hold the points of the object being drawn ($84F0). In play the tile corners are copied from the cache at $BC00-$CBFF ($385D), otherwise computed at $289D. Stale values in the image.

point_yaw_hi + 1, the next corner along a row. Written directly only at $27C7, which sets the right-hand corners of the tile the player stands on to 20, the right edge of the view, so that tile fills the bottom of the screen (its left corners get $FF, far left, at $27BF and $27BC).
point_yaw_hi + 32: the second half of the tile-corner entries, the other row of the pair (entries 32-63). $27BC puts $FF (far left) here for the left corner of the player's own tile.
point_yaw_hi + 33: the next corner in the second half; $27C4 puts 20 (the right edge of the view) here for the player's own tile.
Entries 64-95 of the yaw high bytes (see $A800): the points of the object being drawn, stored from $84F0 as $8475 works through the object's points. Stale in the image.

Not the game's: 484 bytes of BBC BASIC at its ROM address, in the place where the BBC original has the maths routines the C64 moved to $9280-$9463. They hold BASIC's logarithm constants in its five-byte float form (log10 e = $7F $5E $5B $D8 $AA at $A869, ln 2 = $80 $31 $72 $17 $F8 at $A86E, then a series), its series evaluator ($A897) and the range reduction for SIN and COS ($A9D3), whose BCS at $A9D7 lands on the error block at $AA38: BRK, error 23, 'Accuracy l', cut short by the game's code at $AA44 (BASIC's message is 'Accuracy lost'). Nothing in the game refers to $A860-$AA43.

Print the character in A with a drop shadow, as on the title and prompt screens. If bit 7 of $0C0F is set, or A is not $20-$7E, A goes straight to OSWRCH ($FFEE, the C64's copy at $8A6B). Otherwise A is written into the shadow sequence at $AA96 (front) and $AAA1 (rear), and the 23 bytes $AAAC down to $AA96 go to OSWRCH, last byte first; X is kept. Reached from $3201 (the end of a digit printer that prints 0 as the letter O) and from $AA6E. The BBC original's instructions, only the addresses moved.

Print one byte of a text token (from $3418, for every token byte below $C8). A PLOT code ($19) goes to OSWRCH with the next five bytes of the token, fetched from $AA96+Y onwards (Y is the token printer's index, left on the last byte), counted down in $AA83 from 6. Any other byte goes to $AA44. No C64 token contains a PLOT any more (the BBC original's tokens 7-9 and 12 did), so that branch goes unused.
Bytes of a PLOT still to send, for $AA6A: 6 at rest ($19 and five parameters), counted down per byte and set back to 6 at the end. With no PLOT in the C64's tokens it stays 6.

Text tokens: 18 offsets; token n's text starts at $AA96 plus the n-th byte. Read by the token printer $8617, which $3414 also calls for a token byte of $C8+n inside another token. Offsets $17-$AC put the tokens at $AAAD-$AB42. Identical to the BBC original's table: the tokens the C64 changed were padded to their old lengths.

Drop-shadow VDU sequence, 23 bytes to $AAAC, sent last byte first by $AA44; its start is also the base of the token offsets at $AA84. In the order sent: a space and a DEL (127), PLOT 0,0,-4 (graphics cursor 4 units down), GCOL 0 with the rear colour ($AAA2), the rear character ($AAA1), a backspace, PLOT 0,0,4 (back up), GCOL 0 with the front colour ($AA97), and this byte, the front character. $AA51 writes the character here before each use; the '?' in the image, like its twin at $AAA1, is the last character printed before the backup was made. The C64's OSWRCH at $8A6B interprets the BBC VDU codes.

Colour byte of the GCOL sent just before the front character; $13B6 sets it (A EOR 3) when a screen is set up. With $AA98-$AAA0 it makes the front half of the shadow sequence, read backwards: backspace, PLOT 0,0,4, GCOL 0 and this colour.
The rear (shadow) character of the sequence, written at $AA54 along with $AA96 before each character.

Colour byte of the GCOL sent before the rear character: $13BC sets it to 2, or to 3 when the front colour is not 0. With $AAA3-$AAAC it makes the start of the sequence, read backwards: space, DEL, PLOT 0,0,-4, GCOL 0 and this colour.

Text token 0 (byte $C8), printed on the title screen at $1027: token 10 (text at the graphics cursor, graphics background colour 0), token 12 (TAB(1,21)), token 17 ('PRESS ANY KEY'), then COLOUR 129 (text background colour 1). Every token ends with $FF.

Text token 1 ($C9), printed at $1037 to ask for a landscape: TAB(1,21) and thirteen spaces (tokens 12, 15, 15, 16) to wipe the prompt row, TAB(1,2) and 'LANDSCAPE' (tokens 7, 13), ' NUMBER?', VDU 4 (text back at the text cursor) and TAB(5,21) for the typed digits. The BBC original puts the digits on row 27.
Text token 2 ($CA), printed at $105F to ask for a secret code: token 10, TAB(1,2), 'SECRET ENTRY CODE' (token 14), '?', VDU 4 and TAB(3,21) for the eight digits. The BBC original puts them on row 27.
Text token 3 ($CB), printed at $1081 after a wrong code: token 10, TAB(1,2), 'WRONG SECRET CODE', then token 0 (PRESS ANY KEY).

Text token 4 ($CC), printed at $8864 over the landscape preview: token 11 (text at the graphics cursor, graphics background colour 1), TAB(3,24), 'PRESS ANY KEY', TAB(1,2), two VDU 9 (cursor right), 'LANDSCAPE' and one more VDU 9, after which the landscape's number is printed.
Text token 5 ($CD), printed at $1AA8 on the screen that shows the next landscape's secret code: TAB(1,2) 'SECRET ENTRY CODE', TAB(3,4) 'LANDSCAPE', VDU 9.
Text token 6 ($CE), printed at $3632 when a landscape has been finished: TAB(1,21) 'PRESS ANY KEY'.

Text token 7 ($CF): TAB(1,2), the heading row, then $FF and three zero bytes never printed. The BBC original's token 7 is a six-byte PLOT moving the graphics cursor to (64,768); the C64 uses a text TAB and pads the token to the old length, so the offsets at $AA84 stayed as they were.
Text token 8 ($D0): TAB(3,4), $FF and three zero pad bytes; the BBC original moves the graphics cursor to (192,704) here.
Text token 9 ($D1): TAB(3,24), $FF and three zero pad bytes; the BBC original moves the graphics cursor to (192,64) here.
Text token 10 ($D2): VDU 5 (text drawn at the graphics cursor) and GCOL 0,128 (graphics background colour 0).
Text token 11 ($D3): VDU 5 and GCOL 0,129 (graphics background colour 1).
Text token 12 ($D4): TAB(1,21), the prompt row, then $FF and three zero pad bytes; the BBC original moves the graphics cursor to (64,160) here.
Text token 13 ($D5): 'LANDSCAPE'.
Text token 14 ($D6): 'SECRET ENTRY CODE'.
Text token 15 ($D7): five spaces.
Text token 16 ($D8): three spaces.
Text token 17 ($D9): 'PRESS ANY KEY', the last token; the music follows.

Music: four tunes, read by the player at $34DE from $AB50 plus the offset $888F is given (0, 25, 50 or 66). A byte of $C8 or more sets the wait after each following note to (byte - $C8) x 4 ticks of the counter $0CDF, which the interrupt counts down at $9630; any other byte is a note, pitch in quarter-semitones (the scale of the table at $9033/$9133), played as sound 3 ($AC18) on the next of the three voices in turn; $FF ends the tune. Notes with no wait between them sound together as a chord. Offset 0, this label: the hyperspace tune (started at $2181 in the hyperspace routine), five chords 8+36+36, 20+48+48, 28+56+56, 0+28+28, 8+36+36, 24 ticks apart, the last left to ring. Byte for byte the BBC original's music.

Music offset 25: the tune for transferring into another robot (started at $1B84): five chords 8+36+36, 20+48+48, 16+44+44, 0+28+28, 8+36+36, 24 ticks apart; only its third chord differs from the hyperspace tune's.
Music offset 50: the game-over tune (started at $87F6): single notes 8, 36, 64 and 68 sixteen ticks apart, 84 held for 60 ticks, then 104, 84, 68, 64 and 36 four ticks apart and a closing 8.

Music offset 66: the tune for finishing a landscape (started at $3627): six three-note chords, 8+36+36, 0+28+28, 28+56+56, 20+48+48, 16+28+28 and 8+36+36, their notes 4 ticks apart, the first five held for 48, 20, 24, 28 and 36 ticks and the last left to ring.

Energy icons and scanner frame: ten multicolour character shapes, 8 bytes each, copied by $98E8 into characters 240-249 of all five play character sets ($4780, $4F80, $5780, $5F80, $6780) and put on the top screen row by $9508 as character 240 + n. This label: character 240, the empty cell of the icon row (every pixel colour 1), and 241, the robot icon worth 3 units ($9536). The C64's own shapes: the BBC original keeps icon bitmaps in its own screen format here.
Characters 242 and 243, side by side the tree icon, 1 unit of energy (placed at $9547-$954E for a remainder of 1).
Characters 244 and 245, side by side the boulder icon, 2 units of energy (a remainder of 2).
Character 246, the gold robot icon, worth 15 units ($951F).

Characters 247, 248 and 249, the scanner box on the top row: 247 at column 29 (a line down its right side), 248 repeated to column 37 (lines along its top and bottom), 249 at column 38 (a line down its left side), placed at $955D-$9570.

Sound blocks: seven 8-byte blocks, sound n at $AC00 + 8n, handed to OSWORD 7 by $3470 (X = low byte, Y = $AC). The C64 uses its own block format, read by its OSWORD handler at $8DB4: voice (0-2); SID control byte (waveform and gate); attack/decay; sustain/release (its low nybble also picks a release time from $8EC1); note, looked up in $9033/$9133; bits 0-3 the pulse width's high nybble, and with bit 7 set the frequency halved (bits 4-6) + 1 times; duration in ticks of $8ED1 ($80 or more: not timed out); offset of a pitch effect at $AC40 ($80: none). Sound 0, this block: an enemy turning, played at $181D after its yaw changes: voice 0, noise, attack/decay $94, note 48 three octaves down, 12 ticks. The BBC original's sound data here is in BBC SOUND and ENVELOPE form.

Sound 1 (format at $AC00): a meanie turning, played at $1750: voice 0, pulse wave (pulse width high nybble 1), attack/decay $94, note 30 three octaves down, 12 ticks. The BBC original passes two pitches for sounds 0 and 1; the C64 plays both blocks as they stand.

Sound 2 (format at $AC00): creating or absorbing, played at $12EE: voice 0, noise, attack/decay $DF, sustain/release $E0, note 100, duration $FF, so it is not timed out and lasts until OSBYTE 21 stops the voice ($8F81) or another sound takes it.

Sound 3 (format at $AC00): the music's notes. For every note the player at $34DE writes the pitch to $AC1C and moves byte 0, the voice, on by one, 0 to 2 in turn ($3504-$3510); $888F starts a tune on voice 1. Sawtooth, attack/decay $0B, sustain/release $2B, 62 ticks, pitch effect 0 ($AC40).
Note byte of sound 3: the pitch of the current music note, written by the player at $34FB.

Sound 4 (format at $AC00), the scanner sound in the BBC original's naming: played at $3568 when $0C73 is 4, then a 50-tick wait ($0CDF): voice 1, sawtooth, attack/decay $DA, sustain/release $8B, note 34, 20 ticks, pitch effect 7 ($AC47).

Sound 5 (format at $AC00): the ping, played after the energy icons change ($1A1F), for a volume key ($34B2) and at $1BB0 with a higher note: voice 2, pulse wave, attack/decay $08, note 144 ($AC2C), 20 ticks, pitch effect 14 ($AC4E).
Note byte of sound 5: 144, except that $1BAB sets 170 for the ping at $1BB0 (where the BBC original sounds an action that is not allowed) and $1BB5 puts 144 back.

Sound 6 (format at $AC00): the game-over sound. The game's end starts it by setting $0C73 to 6: $87C4-$87CB, in the end-of-game screen routine at $87B1, also sets the note in $0C74 to 230, and $35EA does it when a hyperspace has ended the game ($0CDE). Played at $354C: voice 0, noise two octaves down, attack/decay $02, 1 tick.

Note byte of sound 6, written at $3547 from $0C74, which starts at 230 ($87CB) and drops by one per sound ($355A) while it is 60 or more, so the noise falls in pitch; the gaps between the sounds are 1 to 4 ticks at random ($354F-$3557).

Not the game's: 8 bytes of BBC BASIC code (STA $0600,Y then LDA $19 / PHA / LDA $1A: BASIC's string buffer and text pointer) between the last sound block and the pitch effects; no block or effect index reaches them.

Pitch effects: three 7-byte records, copied into the sound handler's own area ($8E62) when a sound block names one in its byte 7 (0, 7 or 14). Byte 0: bit 7 set = run once, clear = repeat; bits 0-1 must match the value passed to $FFC5 ($8F19; the interrupt passes 3 at $963A, so every record runs). Bytes 1-3: the step added to the note in each of three phases (signed, in quarter-semitones); bytes 4-6: how many ticks each phase lasts (0 skips it). $8F0C steps them once a tick. This record, effect 0, for the music (sound 3): +1 for a tick, -1 for a tick, then 8 ticks unchanged, repeating: a flick of the pitch every ten ticks.
Pitch effect 7 (format at $AC40), for sound 4, the scanner: +6 and -6 on alternate ticks, repeating, so the note warbles between itself and a tone and a half higher.
Pitch effect 14 (format at $AC40), for sound 5, the ping: +1 for two ticks, -1 for one, then 7 ticks unchanged, run once (bit 7 of byte 0), so the ping ends one step above its note.

Not the game's: 43 bytes of BBC BASIC code between the pitch effects and the sine table, part of BASIC's expression reader: it tests for a '+' sign and moves back the text pointer offset in $1B. Nothing in the game refers to $AC55-$AC7F.

Sine table, a quarter wave in 128 bytes: entry n is 256 x sin(n x 90/128 degrees), rounded, capped at 255. $0F70 reads the sine and the cosine of an angle at once (entries n and 128 - n, 128 read as 127) into $8E/$8F, swapped according to the quadrant; the caller takes the signs from $67. This label: entries 0-63, 0 to 44.3 degrees, values 0 to 179. Byte for byte the BBC original's.
Sine table entries 64-127 (see $AC80): 45 to 89.3 degrees, values 181 to 255; entries 120-127 are all 255, the last five because 256 does not fit in a byte.

Run-time workspace, 256 bytes, with two uses. In play: the left x-coordinate of the polygon being filled on each pixel line, indexed by the line ($2EB2, and the edge tracer's self-modified STX at $311F and $317E); the right edges are at $AE00, and $22BA and $237A compare the two. While a landscape is generated: the strip workspace, $2AD1 filling $AD00-$AD50 with 81 numbers from the landscape's seed generator ($31CA) and $2BD5-$2C73 smoothing a strip of tile altitudes in place, with the block list at $AD40. The BBC original uses its $5A00 the same two ways. The image holds bytes left from an earlier run.
polygon_left_x + 1: the next tile along a strip, for the smoothing code ($2BE1, $2C13, $2C36).
polygon_left_x + 2: the tile after next along a strip, for the smoothing code ($2BE4, $2BF2, $2C10, $2C3E).

polygon_left_x + 3: the fourth tile of the window that $2C32-$2C54 averages (four neighbouring tiles added and divided by four); the bytes on to $AD2D are more of the strip in generation and more left edges in play.

polygon_left_x + 46, used as $AD2E,X with X = 32 at $2C5C: it copies seed byte $AD4E, the 79th of the 81 at $AD00, into the operand of the LDA #0 at $0F3C ($0F3D), as the BBC original does for an anti-cracker check (its CheckCrackerSeed, C64 $322F). Otherwise part of the strip and edge workspace.

During landscape generation: a list of numbers of the 4x4 tile blocks whose highest tile is at a given altitude, built at $15A9 and read at $1525 when enemies are placed. In play: more of the left-edge table (see $AD00).

Not a fixed reference: $2FAD is a STX whose operand $2F71-$2F74 set at run time, so the address in the image ($AD7C) is only where the last polygon edge was stored. The bytes from here are more of the left-edge table (see $AD00).

Run-time workspace, 256 bytes, with two uses. In play: the right x-coordinate of the polygon being filled on each pixel line ($2EB7, and the edge tracer's self-modified STX at $2F5F), compared with the left edges at $AD00 by $22B7 and $2377. While a landscape is generated: the highest altitude in each 4x4 block of tiles at $AE10, and the x and z of that highest tile at $AE60 and $AEA0. The BBC original uses its $5B00 the same way. The image holds bytes left from an earlier run.
block_max_altitude - 9: one row back and one column left of block X on the 8-wide grid of 4x4 tile blocks; $152A zeroes it when an enemy has been put in block X, so no second enemy lands next to it.
block_max_altitude - 8: the block one row back from block X, zeroed at $152D with its neighbours.
block_max_altitude - 7: one row back and one column right of block X, zeroed at $1530; the bytes to $AE0E are more of the right-edge table in play.
block_max_altitude - 1: the block to the left of block X, zeroed at $1533.

During landscape generation: the highest tile altitude in each 4x4 block of tiles, one byte per block for an 8 by 8 grid ($AE10-$AE4F), found at $15D0-$1610 and read at $15A1; once an enemy is placed in a block, $152A-$1542 zero that block and its eight neighbours (offsets -9 to +9). In play: part of the right-edge table (see $AE00).
block_max_altitude + 1: the block to the right of block X, zeroed at $1539; the bytes to $AE16 are blocks 1-6 of the table.
block_max_altitude + 7: one row on and one column left of block X, zeroed at $153C.
block_max_altitude + 8: the block one row on from block X, zeroed at $153F.
block_max_altitude + 9: one row on and one column right of block X, zeroed at $1542; from here to $AE4F is the rest of the 64-block table, and the zeroing can reach 9 bytes past it.

During landscape generation: the tile x-coordinate of the highest tile in each 4x4 block (64 bytes, in the order of $AE10), written at $161B and read at $1545 to put an enemy there. In play: part of the right-edge table (see $AE00).

Not a fixed reference: the STX at $2F5F has its operand's low byte ($2F60) counted down at $2F62 as the right-edge tracer works up the polygon, so $AE77 is only where the last trace stopped. The bytes from here are part of the x-coordinate table of $AE60 and of the right-edge table.
During landscape generation: the tile z-coordinate of the highest tile in each 4x4 block (64 bytes), written at $1620 and read at $154A. In play: part of the right-edge table (see $AE00).

Missing from this copy ($B000-$B5FF holds a fill pattern; excluded in game.json). Called once per scroll step of a pan from the loop at $3668-$3692, which replaces the BBC original's wait for its interrupt-driven scroll: the interrupt sets bit 7 of $0CD8 each frame while the step counter $0CC1 is not 0 ($964F-$9656), $96A6 moves the view offsets ($94-$96) and counts $0CC1 down ($972A), the raster is checked against line 230 ($3670), then this is called. So it must move the picture for one step; what it moves, and where, is unknown.

Run-time cache, added by the C64 version: the angles at which every one of the 32 x 32 tile corners is seen from the centre of the player's tile. Four 1 KB tables laid out like the tile map at $0400 (corner (x, z) at offset (x AND 3) x 256 + (x DIV 4) x 32 + z): yaw low byte here, yaw high byte at $C000, pitch low and high bytes, divided by 16, at $C400 and $C800. $3700 fills all four with GetHypotenuseAngle ($9287); the main game loop calls it at $35BD right after the tile-visibility pass ($245B), and skips both after a U-turn (bit 7 of $0C51), when the player has not moved. While bit 7 of $9AF6 is set (play), the tile-angle routine ($283D) jumps to $37F2, which only subtracts the view's current yaw and pitch from these; the BBC original works each corner's angles out as it draws. The image holds a fill pattern here.
Tile-corner angle cache (see $BC00): yaw high byte of every corner as seen from the player's tile, written at $3777; $3859 subtracts the view's yaw ($B2) from it into $A800.
Tile-corner angle cache (see $BC00): pitch low byte of every corner, after the pitch has been divided by 16 ($37C7-$37E1); $3860 subtracts the view's pitch ($B0) from it into $0A80.
Tile-corner angle cache (see $BC00): pitch high byte of every corner, divided by 16 with its sign kept (written at $37DD); $3868 subtracts $B1 from it into $0AE0.

JMP $8ED1, written at start by $8959-$895B with its operand from $891D-$8924; excluded, $FF in this copy. The address is the BBC's GSINIT entry; the C64 uses it for its once-a-frame note timer ($8ED1: durations and releases of the three voices), called from the interrupt at $963D.
Low byte of the JMP at $FFC2, $D1, written at $891F.
High byte of the JMP at $FFC2, $8E, written at $8924.

JMP $8F0C, written at start by $895E; excluded, $FF in this copy. The address is the BBC's GSREAD entry; the C64 uses it for its once-a-frame pitch-effect stepper ($8F0C, records at $AC40), called from the interrupt at $963A with A = 3.
Low byte of the JMP at $FFC5, $0C, written at $8929.
High byte of the JMP at $FFC5, $8F, written at $892E.
JMP $8D2C, written at start by $8964, at the address of the BBC's OSRDCH (read a character); called at $862C. Excluded, $FF in this copy.
Low byte of the JMP at $FFE0, $2C, written at $893D.
High byte of the JMP at $FFE0, $8D, written at $8942.

JMP $8A6B, written at start by $8961, at the address of the BBC's OSWRCH (write a character): the C64's VDU interpreter, used by the text printers ($AA44, $AA6A) and others. Excluded, $FF in this copy.
Low byte of the JMP at $FFEE, $6B, written at $8933.
High byte of the JMP at $FFEE, $8A, written at $8938.

JMP $8D81, written at start by $8967, at the address of the BBC's OSWORD: the C64's handler takes A = 7 (play a sound block, $8DB4, blocks at $AC00) and A = 10 (copy a character's 8 bytes from the font at $8000, $8D8A); anything else returns. Excluded, $FF in this copy.
Low byte of the JMP at $FFF1, $81, written at $8947.
High byte of the JMP at $FFF1, $8D, written at $894C.

JMP $8F78, written at start by $896A, at the address of the BBC's OSBYTE: the C64's handler takes A = $81 (scan the keyboard, $8CF9) and A = $15 (silence voice X, $8F81); anything else returns, including the $7E sent at $8639. Excluded, $FF in this copy.
Low byte of the JMP at $FFF4, $78, written at $8951.
High byte of the JMP at $FFF4, $8F, written at $8956.
